(Concluded ) A ROMANCE OF THE PASSING ERA With pecuniary means supplied by Mr Rymer, Hume went to Paris in July, accompanied by Mr þÿRymer son, s and nominally as the young þÿman s tutor. Some American gentlemen then took him along with them to Florence, where he spent the winter, and astonished many English residents with his marvels. Here, however, a revolution took place in his mind. He became convinced that the phenomena in America, however Veritable, were of a discommendable nature, in as far as they had not in general a religious aspect. The doctrines of the Catholic church, recommended to him probably by the affinity of the so-called miracles of the saints to his own mysterious gifts were embnucd by him. The priests, however, condemned the exercise of his alleged control of spoils, and he soon after announced that the power had suddenly deserted him. On the 27th of March 1856, he was received into the Catholic church. At first, he feared that he should again be thrown destitute ; bur a Polish nobleman now took him up, and conducted him to Puris, where he remain, d for several months in low health and devoid of his former power. During the ensuing month, Mr Hume and his spirits were the reigning topic of Paris. In the presence of the emperor, the empress, and a very small

and select party, many of the marvels previously described are alleged to have taken place, leaving impressions of mingled wonder and suspicion. The emperor beheld all with his characteristic nonchalance, and never allowed an expression of assent to drop from his lips. It hits been stated, however, that, on his saying, evening that he could not be convinced of the presence of a spirit unless lie should receive from one some raps on the shoulder, immediately some hard blows were given him in that quarter. She put her handkerchief, Spanish fashion, under her garter, and desired Hume to ask his spirits to tell where it was. Three gentlemen on one occasion played a trick upon him, which was at first rather damaging, because it raised a laugh against him. DEATH OF M EXTERN 10 II. þÿ Thedeath of Mettcrnich marks a period in the history of the þÿworld politics, s lie was the last great professor of the art of impudent sham. Some pupils survive, carrying out the doctrine as far as they are allowed, but he was the last instance of a haughty and, almost up to the hour of his death, a triumphant assertion of the principle that the many are made for the few. The same conscience that bade one of the Counts of Luxemburg set his nephew to hack defenceless prisoners to pieces that lie might learn the art of bloodshed, inspired Mcttcrnich in all his dealings on behalf of the House of Hapsburg to its subjects. He had not the slightest notion that the happiness of mankind is the object of Government. If he eared for it at all, it was as the accessory to prosperous autocracy, llis pupil Buol gives the finest possible exemplification of the doctrine in the diplomatic correspondence just published by tbe Derby Cabinet. Buol resents t lie notion that the English Government should toll France or Sardinia that Italy had anything 1 ft nlon chievous. Italy would remain quiet if it were to complain of. . Whether the Italians were misera- That was dangerous and misble or not, whether they throve or perished, was a peifectly irrelevant affair. The great object was, that they should not disturb the repose of their betters. They were made to suffer "r to lie relieved, ns it might suit the whim or the disregarding onward course of their owners. To take their welfare into an

aeonunt was an impertinence which Buol only did not resent because at the time it wnsnecessarv to lie civil to England. The miserable pupil is dismissed and the wretched master dies about the same time ; and both from the same cause, that light has become too strong for them It is satisfactory to learn that þÿMetternicb death s was hasteued j by the news of the patriotic success in Italy. | \Yo write this in no poor spirit of vengeance. It is well that it should he recorded that the old instrument of tyranny died of his crimes. He was executed by discomfiture and his own impotent malice. \Vc have no wish to pursue ( . him beyond the grave ; our retribution cannot xteud so far; hut on earth it is mercy as wed as justice to devote his memory to execration. Loathed, accursed, and despised for ever he the remembrance of all tyranny, that the pride of tyrants may shrink from incurring the doom ! Let the howl and screech over þÿMetternicb s grave make his imitators tremble. Not presuming to enter on þÿ the judgment to þÿcome, it lias yet at times interested us to conjecture how the mere hard egotists, the Napoleon the Firsts and the Metternichs, for example, who have exulted in the pride of the craft they have mistaken for high intellect, must, on coming to the truth, be aghast to find themselves the objects of utter contempt as well as of unmitigated abhorrence. þÿ It was for the wretched rag of such power as you won that you caused all this misery þÿ! is the jeer of history here

and of a much more searching and terrible opinion elsewhere. The war goes on, and the Austrians retreat so fast that their great patron, the Times , jests at their new-found alaciity. Cruel sport, hut quite natural from such friends. We, too, wish to sec it endod. Let the poor victims of despotism go home from their sad suffering and sadder work. We trust especially that the Prince Regent of Prussia will act as his official journals promise for him. Let him mobilise liis army as a measure of precaution, as much against German panic and reckless princeling idiocy as against the arms of the French. Let him take full care of the security of his lucklessly scattered and exposed territory, as we do for our compact sea-girt limits. But let

THE NOBLES OF ROME. As soon as t hey shall have passed their last examinations, and obtained tiicir diplomas of ignorance, they will be dressed in the latest Loudon fashions, and he turned out into the public promenades. They will pace for ever the pavement of the Coi so, they will weai out tlie a. leys of t o 1'iucian Hill, the Villa Borghe-e, aud ti.e Villa þÿ1 iinphili.They will rule, þÿUriv. and , walk about, armed with whip, eye g a-s, or cane, as may he, until they are made to mairy. Regular at Mass, assiduous at the theatre, you may s e them smile, gape, equal applaud, m ike the sigu of toe cross, with all absence ol emotion. They are almost an iusenbed on the list of some religious fraternity or other. They belong to no club, play timidly, ran-ly make a parade of social irregularities, drink without enthusiasm, and never ruiu themselves by horse-racing. In short, their general conduct is beyond all praise; aud the life of dolis made to say þÿ þÿPapa! aud þÿ þÿMama! is equally irreproachable. One fine day they attain their twenty-filth year. At this ago, an American has already tiied his hand at a dozen trades, made lour fort utu s, and at least one bankruptcy, has goue through a couple of campaign-, had a lawsuit, established a new religious sect, killed half-a-dozen men with his revolver, freed a negress, and conquered an island An Englishman has passed some siiff examinations, been attached to an embassy, founded a factory, converted a Catholic, goue round the world, and read the complete works

| of Walter Scott. A Frenchman has rhymed a tragedy, written fur two newspapers, been wounded in three duels, twice attempted suicide, vexed fourteen husbands, and changed his politics nineteen times. A German has slashed

fifteen of his dearest friends, swallowed sixty hogsh ads of beer and the Philosophy of Hegel, sui g eleven thousand couplets, compromised a tavern waning-inaid. smoked a million of pipes, and he. n mixed up with, at least, two revolutions. The Roman prince has done nothing, seen nothing, learnt nothing, loved nothing, suffered nothing. His parents or guardians open a cloister gate, take out a young girl as inexperienced as himself, aud the pair of innocents are bidden to kneel before a priest, who gives them permission to become the parents of another gem ration of innocents like themselves. Probably you expect to find them living unhappily together. Not at all. And yet the wile is pretty. The monotonous routine of her convent education has not so frozen her heart that she is incapable of loving ; her uncultivated mind will spontaneously develop itself when it comes in contact with the world. She will not fail, ere long, to discover the inferiority of her husband. The more her education lias been neglected, the greater is her chance of remaining womanly, that is to say, intelligent, tender and charming. In truth, the harmony of their household is less likely to be disturbed at Rome than it would be at Paris or Vienna. þÿ The Roman Question. By M. About. o þÿ þÿ FR OM WA SUING TON.

Although the Paraguay squadron returned from the scene of its þÿpeaoel ul exploits unharmed, and boastful of having performed its mission without firing a gun, the official disclosures are well calculated to provoke the severest criticism and reprehension. Commodore Shubrick, who commanded the expedition, required the subordinates charged with the various departments to report to him in detail, so that the information thus collected might be of service to the Government, should any like necessity occur. Among the official reports thus made, is one showing that the ammunition provided would have only lasted seven hours with rapid firing. The hare mention of such a fact, whicli cannot be successfully disputed, carries its owu commentary This expedition was fitted out at a large cost, aud especially lor a hostile purpose, and yet alter reaching the distant destination in tho þÿenemy s country, it was found to be almost wholly unprovided with the means of aggression or defense. This is no fancy sketch, and is couccived in no factious spirit. It involves a most serious and important question, which cannot be ignored or answered by the usual partisan declamation. Suppose Lopez had decided upon resistance, and not yielded to the counsels of the neighboring nations, what a spectacle would we have presented to tbe civilized world after the first j seven hours of battle ! Every vessel that escaped the Para uayau forts and guns would have been compelled to retreat and wait the arrival of am-

munition from home, or buy it in South America. if purchasable. True, we escaped this possible predicament, but with nono the less discredit tor criminal omissions, whicli must be investigated next Winter. In the first place, o ir officers and men are sent five thousand miles away in canal boats and other uuscaworthy cratt, thus imperiling their lives for a pecuniary speculation, and then when they reach Paraguay the fir-t essentials of hostile operations are wanting. Those steamers were a constant subject of ridicule everywhere, and it is well known to all professional men that a single Minnie ball might have disabled any one of them by perforating the steam chests, which loomed up as targets above tbe water line. It was a providential dispe, nation that none of them encountered hard weather nr the cyclone, in which the Sabine was nearly lost. As it was, they broke down with smooth seas going out, and required two months to reach Paraguay under steam. Commodore Shubrick ordered them home in couples as the only inode ot -afety, so that one might help the other as they became alternately disabled, and the Chapin was actually towed five thousand miles. Tbe Metacomet was condemned in Paraguay alter a survey, with one hundred holes in her boilers, as the report states. Yet she was hired at $3,500 a month, though purchased for $4,000 before being imposed on the Government Suclt scandalous mismanagement and enf able neglect of the plainest duty cannot bo too strongly condemned, and will form the basis
ot an investigation, and perhaps something else, before many months. þÿ New York Tribune

AMERICAN OPINION ON THE WAR IN EUROPE. Within the past six years there have been three great wars in which European nations have engaged þÿ tho Crimean war, the war in India, and the present war in Italy. In none of these had the United States any interest, direct or remote; but the people of the United States felt and expressed decided sympathies for one side or the other in eaoh of them A

study of tlie facts goes to show that Americans, as a rule, are much less influenced by th -ir prejudices than is commonly supposed, hut are which, nevertheless, might not always be exercise governed by principles which, to p rliaps, they prepared general sway over define, but the mind of the nation. Daring the Crimean war the sympa lee of this country were unequivocally with Russia. There were a few pres-es and peisons here nd there þÿ connected in one way or another with England or France þÿ whose feelings were on the side of the Allies. There w.is no pi in ip e involved in the war. Liberty was n t a stake on either side. As between ihe hostile nations, in view of humanity, there was u thing to choose: the Zouaves are as savage as die t ossacks, and the English sacked the museum at Kertch. The English papers tried hard to show that the war was one of civilization against barbarism ; but this ridiculous assumption imposed on no one. Americans saw plainly enough that the Turk was at least as birbirous as the Russian, aud that civilisation had liitle to expect from success ou cither side. Driven, therefore, to their þÿwits end to accoum for ihe decided sympathies ielt by Americans for tbe Russians, the writers who examined tnesabj ct came to the conclusion that we were biased by

latent jealousy of England and anti British prejudice. We arc ol opinion that the judgment was unwarranted, and that i s audio. s ascrib'd undue influence to certain Iiish orators and petty politicians, who, they supposed, had been the means of exciting that jealousy and that prejudice. Wo are inclined to think that the American sympathy for Russit gr. w altog di. r out of the beliefþÿ which was gen ial in ibis country þÿ that the war was unnecessary, that Russia was overmatched, ami tnat two poweriul maritime Powers had clubbed together to buly and humiliate a third. It is a fact t. at s > lo. g as the war was confined to Turkey, ur sympathies were with tne Turk-; dunng the wh lo of Omar þÿPacha s campaign on the Danube Russia had no friends in tuis country. It was only when the Allies landed and concentrated their infernal þÿtire ou Sebastopol; when Todtloben, by prodigies of genius, withstood the assaults cf euemits infinitely superior to him in numbers, in guns, and in i ce urecs of every kind; when the Russians died by the thousand a day, but held firm to their fortress þÿ was it mly then that American sympathy pronounced itself decidedly in favor of Russia. We infer from these facts that that sympathy was merely the natural feeling awakened by heroic lesistaneo against overwhelming odds, that it implied no particular liking for Russia, aud no extreme prejudice agaiust England. This view is confirmed by the decided sympathy felt throughout this country for Great Brit mi iti the war in India. On the face of it,

it would not have seemed unnatural had our people sympathized with the Hindoos who appeared to be lighting for independence and liberty. Rut the contempt and loathing elicited by one nr t.wn Irish demonstrations in favor of the Sepoys showed clearly which way the tide of feeling flowed ; and the honors paid to the memory of Havelock afforded a still more emphatic illustration of our sympathy with England. The secret of this very singular fact will be found in the general conviction among Americans that the Hindoo is incapable of maintaining unaided even the imperiect civilization sustained by the English in India; that his success would have been the prelude to an era of barbarism and bloodshed ; und that the English raj, with all its faults, was stiseep

The sympathy based upon these principhs was assisted by the Sepoy atrocities; but its real basis was what wo have stated. It is in that j view of the question, and in view of the effect which such a contingency may have upon tho Caiholio church throughout the world, that indications of the leanings of Pio Nono in this war become highly interesting and important. There is no doubt that although Louis Napoleon sent an army to Rome in lb4S to expel Garibaldi and the tribunes, and lo restore the head of the Catholic church to his seat in the Eternal City, his feelings were then and are now averse to the continued existence of the popedom as a temporal sovereignty. That movement was dictated by high considerations ol policy rather

than by a desire to perpetuate the existing Papal system ; on the contrary, one of the leading Napoleonic ideas is to restrict the Pope to his mere spiritual sway, and to relieve him of all the weighty questions of State which must from time to time devolve upon even the smallest and weakest of sovereignties. That idea has probably become a fixed principle in the mind of the French Emperor ; and therefore there may have been good ground for the rumor which obtained publicity at the outbreaking of this war, to the eff ct that one of þÿNapoleon plans s was to put an mid to the þÿPope t s emporal power, to take from under his control the whole of the Pupal States, but to have him the city of Rome and endow him with an annual stipend sufficient for the maintenance of his high position. Now, whatever good Catholics and liberal men of all denominations may think as to the advisability of such a change in regard to the head of the Catholic church, there is no good reason to belf ve that tho project finds favor either with Pius ihe Ninth or his Council ol Ministers And therefore it is not to be wondered at that the sympathies of the Court of Rome are with I the Austiians in this contest, and that in the eyes of that Couit Austrian domination seems preferable to Italian independence

Those sympathies are not without expression The Pope, although he has proclaimed the nou trality of his government in the existing struggle, makes no secret of his leanings in favor of Austria, and has permitted that Power to fortify Ancona and other places within his dominions. Again the same desire was manifested, without any such excuse, but this time Goyon informed his Holiness that lie could not permit him to leave Rome. the early days of napoleon. There hangs over the boyish days of Napoleon Bonaparte a mystery somewhat similar to that which rests on the opening years of Shakspeare. In case of the latter, we are totally at a loss to comprehend by what species of training that wonderful mind was developed, and whence was derived that boundless knowledge of human nature, and of the phenomena of the universe, which his writings display. With the like feelings of uncertainty do we muse upon the early life of Napoleon, wondering in what manner that prodigious amount of intelligence was accumulated which gave him such a sway in after-days over his fellow-men, and rendered him never for one instant at a loss, amid the most varied and trying circumstances in which man could be called upon to act. Bonaparte appeared to burst at once upon the world with the experience of fifty lives concentrated in his young mind, ready to take up at will the parts ol warrior, ruler, legislator, or diplomatist, and to cope with and foil those who had grown gray in studying the duties of but one or other of these dif ficult characters. These circumstances throw a peculiar interest over the youth of Napoleon. Fortunately, during the period of the Consulate, he gave directions for the preservation of various letters and papers connected with his early history, and from a notice of these, published some years ago in France, we shall proceed to draw several particulars. Paoli, the Corsican patriot, seems to have been a material instrument in mould-

ing the character of the young Napoleon. Genoa had assumed the right of selling Corsica to France, in the time of Louis XV., and that monarch sent an army to take possession of it. The Corsicans resisted, under the guidance of Paoli. Charles Bonaparte was a warm partisan of that chief ; and, in the campaign of 1769, which gave France the ascendancy, was personally in the field with his wife Letitia, who, at that very time, in the midst of peril and alarm, gave birth to Napoleon. During the childhood of the latter, Paoli was constantly in the mouths of those around him, and he grew up with a deep admiration of the, character of the exiled general then living in England. When the French Revolution broke out, Paoli was recalled, and Napoleon became his close personal friend. The old general had penetration enough to discern the remarkable character of the youth. ' You are one of Plutarch's men,' he used to say to him þÿ a compliment of no slight kind. It has been often asserted, that Napoleon never acted under the impulse of feeling, but was always guided by motives of selfinterest and cold calculation. Not so was it when Paoli, having incurred the suspicion of the French Convention for his denunciations of the execution of Louis XVI. was summoned to appear and answer for himself in Paris. Napoleon, who had then received a commission in the French service in Corsica, had the generous boldness to write to the Convention in his old friend's defence. ' One of your decrees,' says the

letter, ' has deeply afflicted the citizens of Ajaccio ; it is that which orders an old man of seventy, loaded with infirmities, to drag himself to your bar, charged, through misunderstanding, as corrupt and ambitious. Representatives ! when the French were governed by a corrupt court, and placed credence neither in virtue nor patriotism, then might it have been said, perhaps, that Paoli was ambitious. It is by despots alone that Paoli should now be deemed ambitious ; at Paris, in the midst of French liberty, he ought, to be regarded In the Rcvm 'Iks Dchs, Mamies.

ft T ft i 0; I) «\ Vy II ft. as the patriarch of freedom, the precursor of your republic ; so will posterity think, and so do the people now believe. We owe to him all, even the happiness of being a portion of the Freuch republic. He ever enjoys our confidence. Repeal your decree, and render us happy.' Napoleon's bold appeal was not listened to, and Paoli was compelled to look for safety to England. Another person who exercised much influence over Napoleon in his youth, was Father Dupuy, sub-principal ol tire school of Brieiine. As became common in the case of Corsican families of respectability, after the island was incorporated with France, Napoleon was sent to the college of Autun at the age of nine, and afterwards to the school of Brieune. Bourrienne mentions, in his memoirs of Bonaparte, that the Emperor never could spell properly ; but he does not tell the reason. The fact was, that Napoleon could not speak a word of French when He he came to the school first mentioned. picked up the tongue through his intercourse with others, but never was taught it grammatically. He was engaged 111 learning the classics, when he ougiit to have been set to the French language by his teachers. His excessively careless penmanship in later days was supposed to be partly affected, in order to hide his faulty orthography. Dupuy, who formed a strong attachment to Napoleon, and was shewn the essays from his pen, did all he could to correct the style and spelling; but the evil was not thoroughly removable. One

of the early essays of Napoleon was a history of Corsica, which was composed in the form of Letters, addressed to the Abbd Raynal. Lucieu Bonaparte mentions this work in his memoirs. 'It was written,' he says, in the vacation ' of 1790, at Ajaccio, and two copies were made of it by myself. One was sent to the Abbd Rayual, who found the composition so remarkable that lie shewed it to Mirabeau. The latter, on returning it, said to Raynal, that this little history seemed to him to indicate a genius of the first order. Napoleon was delighted with these praises.' The work was represented by Lucien as lost, but in reality it is still in existence, having formed part of a bundle of early writings lodged by Napoleon in the hands of Cardinal Fescii. It is written with great vigour, and an uncompromising boldness of speech. Every page proves, moreover, that the author had been indefatigable in his researches into authorities, and even unpublished documents. Napoleon's mode of reading books was peculiar, and well calculated to fix on his memory whatever fell under his eye. His custom was to read with the pen in his hand, and to mark pussages which he approved disapproved ; or and frequently, when he was especi .lly struck with anything, he made it the subject of a distinct critical disquisition. Iu this manner did he go over all the most grave arid learned works in the stores of literature. Herodotus, Strubo, Plutarch, and all the otiier historians both of Greece and Rome ; the annals of England, and all

I the most important modern countries in j the world ; natural history, geography, medicine, and physics þÿ all of these branches of learning his papers shew him to have studied attentively. But, above all, his favourite authors were Filarigieri, Mably, Necker, Smith, and other writers on political economy, legislation, and the moral sciences g ner&lly. For seven years þÿ The terms of sale to be seen at the Vennamely, from 1786 to 1793, while a student and lieutenant of artillery, now iu one place and now in another þÿ such was the training to which his papers shew him to have subjected himself. Men have marvel-

led that the soldier of Italy should have started up, as it seemed, a legislator by intuition þÿ intuition! such is the word under which men too frequently shelter their own apathy and deficiencies. Yearn of patient study, while other lads were fooling away their time, would, at least in this instance, have been a more correct form of expression. Napoleon's ability as a soldier was not less puzzling; but comprehensiveness and promptitude of thought, produced by the same preparatory studies, united with a sound physical development, formed the true explanation of the phenomenon. What is curious, however, Bonaparte sometimes left his grave studies for the slightest of all varitios of literary composition : he wrote novels. One of these was an English romance, entitled The Earl of Essex , being founded on the story of Queen Elizabeth's unfortunate favourite. Another tale was composed by him on a Corsican subject, and he also wrote some Otiental apologues, bearing covertly on the politics of the passing day. The idea of the man who wielded such mighty elements in afterdays, devoting time to story-writing, is startling enough. It has the same apparent incongruity as the idea of his being glad to borrow a few shillings from Bourrienne in the days of his lieutenantship. (To be continued.)

THE PEACE. The most striking comment on this last work of Napoleon III. is to be drawn from the correspondence of his hitherto enthusiastic advocate, the Morning Post. The Paris correspondent of that journal writes on " In order to correct the Thursday con- impossibilities : þÿ tained in certain articles of the treaty of peace contracted by the Emperor Napoleon and Francis Joseph, communications are taking place betweeu the Governments of Eng and, France, Prussia, Russia, and Austria, to get up a Congress, which will probably meet at London. Austria, I learn, thinks there is no necessity for a CoDgress ; and well she may. A council of Ministers took place to-day at St Cloud as early as 9 o'clock. Despatches have reached Paris stating that the whole of Italy is greatly agitated The Pope has sent for assistance, in the shape of troops, to the Emperor Napoleon and 1 rancis Joseph. Count Cavour and the whole of the Cabinet have resigned. The King has been advised to call about him a Papal and retrograde Cabinet. There is likely to be political disturbances in Turin The King of Sardinia has arrived in Milan. Hts Majesty will, it is expected, renounce his title to Lombardy, and in all probability abdicate. The Emperor Napoleon has ordered all war preparations to cease. The French army will return home immediately. The Prussian Government has assured that of France that the army will not be sent to the Rhine. Discontent in Paris at the Emperor's proclamation and fears of a

revolt in Italy have caused the funds to fall again to-day, as well as all other securities. I am sorry to say we are expecting to hear of fresh complications in Italy. The terms on which the two Emperors have made peace are sure to give dissatisfaction At a moment, too, when the Italians arc politically excited, and with arms in their hands, one can scarcely iiope tranquility will be maintained. Wherever one turns danger presents itself. The people of the Roman States will have little faith in the Sovereign Pontiff's power or will to make reforms. Only the other day his Holiness declared changes impossible from the very centre of ecclesiastical authority. The Tuscans will scarcely accept the Grand Duke after his flight to the Austrian camp ; the people of Modena and Parma cannot see their rulers return ; and the Venetians will laugh at the idea of a Confederation, in which Austria has a majority of votes, doing them any good. These considerin official quarters, and news from Italy is anxiety ations are causing much uneasiness and looked forward to, I may say, with fear. The Mazzinian party will now say, What do you now think of " the Emperor Napoleon ? He has made a federal Italy, which he gives to Austria and the Pope !' It is the one great, and may be fatal, blunder of the Emperor's life. He has made Austria stronger than ever in Italy, and crowned her power with the cross keys of St Peter's. He has done so in the hour of victory, and when the blood spilt in attempting to cany out his

own programme demands a completion of the great tasks with every prospect of success. The Proclamation which was this day posted up was received, I have no hesitation in with displeasure, and in some instances saying, it was torn down. The conditions on which the war has been closed have produced a painful dissatisfaction in all classes who feel for the national honor of France, and who are real friends of the Emperor Napoleon. I believe the day will come when it shall be proved that the has been deceived as to the state of Emperor feeling in Europe. FRANCE. Pans, Friday, July 15, 6 p. m. re.IBD0.w no mistake about the matter. Invaltdes announced 1 his is the third day that since the cannon of the war was at an end ; the first enthusiasm at the restoration of peace

bag passed off ; aud it is now admitted on all bands that never have gigantic preparations produced more paltry effects. In the first burst of gladness at the carnage being over, the Pays and Constitutioniul alone sang the military and civil genius of the Emperor, and rose in their encomiums, like the shepherds in Virgil's eclogue, or the bidders at an auction, above each other. The hymn of praise, however, has become more subdued ; the Constitutionnel is even obliged to enter into explanations, correct enough, I believe, or to apologize for the result of the magnificent promise of May last. The Patrie itself, in spite of its obligation to praise everything Governmental, kept silt nee for some days, and left the famous despatch standing alone in its first column, cold and shivering, without a paragraph of approbation to warm it. Even now its forced praise is i most measured ; it begins thus : þÿ " No one is more happy than we are at the return of peace. If it does not realize all we expected, never- , theless,'' &c. In fact, the ft eling of mortification increases instead of diminishing ; it is euri- ( ous that it is even stronger among women than men So puzzled are people to account for a denouement so much out of proportion with the design, that the strangest motives are assigned for it. They attribute it to some second projected family alliance between the Imperial family of France and ODe ot the Italian Sovereigns The writer of a letter from Beine of the 1 4th, published in the Presse , mentions that

he heard the Duchess of Parma say, on the 10th, before the peace was signed, that 6he should be in Parma and in possession of her crown before six weeks were over. If M. Cavour has any feeling left, bow keen must be his sense of humiliation, and how bitter his remorse ! He destroyed with his own hand the liberties of his country as the preliminary step to her political humiliation ; and her independence now actually depends on the will of her ally. It is reported that Florence and other pence and that the Pope has refused the " ho- parts of Tuscany have protested against tho norary Presidency" of the Italian Confederation. In a word, Italy, to liberate and organize which the war was undertaken, promises to be soon in a worse state of convulsion than ever. The Ihbdti gives the following explanations of what it conceives to be the most probable arrangement of the Italian States tinder the new organization : þÿ A comparison of the despatch by which the Emperor Napoleon made known the bases of peace adopted at Villafratica with that by which the Emperor of Austria communicated the same event to bis suljects gives a complete idea of the stipulations made by the two Soveleigns. While informing us that Austria is to retain Venetia, the French despatch did not indicate what would be the new froutier between Piedmont and Austria The Austrian despatch mentions the line of the Mincio, which removes all uncertainty as to the fate of Peschiera and Mantua, which remain in the hands of Austria.

The French despatch said nothing about the duchies, and the Emperor's proclamation to the army of Italy only alluded to them in speaking of the Governments which had kept aloof from the movement, or were recalled into their possessions. The Austrian despatch expressly stipulates the restoration of the Sovereigns of Tuscany and Modena. The despatch does not mention the Duchess-Regent of Parma, but it appears to us so much less probable that i she is not included in this general restoration, that, of all the Sovereigns restored, the Duchess- Regent is the ouo who will experience the least embarrassment in again meeting her people. Lastly, the Austrian despatch docs not represent the establishment of a Confederation as an accomplished fact, but merely state that Austria agrees with France in promoting the formation oi' an Italian Confederation. That stipulation thus becomes perfectly intelligible, for it suggests that the assent of the States which are to enter into the proposed confederation will be applied for, and that they cannot be regarded as definitively engaged by arrangements in which they have hitherto had no share Admitting, therefore, in conformity with the opinion of a great number of persons, that there will no CoDgres6, and that Europe will not be called on to give an opinion on the bases adopted at Villafrsnca, there still remain

But that is a work which the rest of Europe, if such be their pleasure, may very properly leave to the parties who signed the preliminaries at Villafrauca, and to Italy, wh. se reorganization they have undertaken together."

NAPLES.

A military revolt, of which the exact causes and objects are yet unknown, broke out at Naples on Thursday week According to the latest accounts, some Swiss troops, having mutinied in the barracks, and killed the Colonel of the 4th Regiment and several officers, alterwards repaired to the Royal palace ; but a battalion of cha.-seurs and a r. giment of hussars, posted there, forced them to fall back as far as the Champ de Mars, where they w. ie surrounded. The General Commander-in-Chief of the Swiss called upon them to surrender; but they replied by a discharge of firearms, wounding the General and about twenty privates. The Nunziantc thin gave oitb is to fire on the mutineers with grape, by which 75 were killed and 233 wounded. 1800 men belonged to the Swiss regiments have been dismissed, and are about to leave for Marseilles, on their way home, with the consent of the French Minister.

At the last meeting the Chairman stated that when the reserved fund amounted to 20,000/ the directors would not think it necessary to appropriate to it so large a proportion of the profit as they had hitherto done. That point having now been attained, aud provision having been made for all bad aud doubtful debts, the directors hope that, should uo unforeseen circumstances arise, they may henceforward be iu a position to recommend a larger distribution ; still, however, gradually adding to the reserved fund until it amounts to a much larger sum than it docs at present. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, stated that it was fortunately of so

favourable a nature as not to require much comment from him ; he would, therefore, not detain them longer than was necessary to answer two questions contained in a letter which had been addressed to him by a proprietor. The first was an enquiry as to the amount of past due bills included in the items, 976,509/. 2s. 10d., in tho balance-sheet. To answer that question distinctly would only he to mislead, unless he went into a detail of what securities they held for a great portion of that sum ; nor did he think the proprietors would call upon him for such a statement. Quarterly returns were received from each manager, and everything considered doubtful or bad was amply provided for. The second question referred to the expediency of distinguishing the profits obtained by each branch. Ho (the Chairman) did not think that such a course would be at all desirable, as they had the competitions of other hanks to contend against. As the reserve fund had reached 50,000/., he was happy to inform the shareholders that it would not be necessary to increase it in the same ratio ; but, at the same time, he would not recommend that the adding to the fund should be entirely discoutiuucd in future years. In reference to the investment of the reserve fund, lie (the Chairman ) said that the bank held Consols and other securities to a much larger amount than the reserved fund, and the shareholders might depend that it was not used in the ordinary cour-e of business, but he shou d be sorry to see it so tied up as to prevent its

use in case it should be necessary at auy future period to do so for the purposes of the bank The report was adopted, and a resolution passed declariug a divided of 4 per cent, for the hall-year. The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman and directors.

(Concluded.) THE EARLY DAYS OF NAPOLEON. We cannot well give a specimen of t lit stories of Napoleon, but in place of these, our space permits of our quoting one of the most remarkable of all his papers. This is a document in which he discusses the propriety of suicide. Many features of his future character seem to hav. nngina ted in youth in his isolated position. Fiom the age of nine to seventeen, he was absent from home. He dwelt alone, and tb oe.i those habits of self-dependence w , . once constituted a great quality in oiiu, a d isolated him in a measure, from human e mpathies. His note-book wastln soleeuiifidaii of his secrets in his youth Whatever- c him forcibly, even a simple conver-a; m with a lady, was committed to paper, and beyond question this plan led him ever to reason coolly before action The following are his thoughts on the subject of selfdestruction : þÿ 'Ever alone in tie midst of men, I return to dream with myself, and to give myself up to all the vivacity of my melancholy. To what point is it now directed ? To the side of death. Yet in the morning of my days, I may hope to live a long time. I have been absent seven years from my country. What pleasure shall I not taste in revisiting, in four months, my relatives and compatriots! Filled with the tender sensations which the remembrance of my youthful pleasures inspires, may I not conclude that my happin- swill be complete? And what inadmss, then, urges me to wish tor my desti ne ion ? Doubtless, 1 may say, Wlitu have I to <io

in this world ? Since 1 must die, is it not as well to end my life ut once ? li 1 inn I passed through sixty years, I should resptct the prejudices of my contemporaries, and wait patiently till nature had completed her course; but since I begin to experience misfortunes, since nothing gives me pleasure, why should I go on enduiing unprosperous days! How fur have men wandered from nature! How cowardiy, base, and servile are they ! What spectacle shall I behold in my native country? My compatriots, loaded with chains, tremblingly kiss the hand which crushes tin m. They are no more those brave Corsicaus, whom a hero animated with his virtues ; no more are they enemies of tyranny, luxury, sycophancy. Proud, ami full of a noble consciousness of worth, a Corsican once lived happy. If he had employed the day on public affairs, his evenings passed away in the sweet society of a loving and beloved spouse; reason and enthusiasm effuced all the fatigues of the day ; tender and natural affection rendered ins nights comparable to those of the gods. But these happy times have disapp hi. <1 with liberty, like passing dreams ! Frenchmen, not content with having reft from uall that we cherished, ye have also co i p ed our manners! The existing specta. e of my country, and my powerlessness io effect a change, form a new reason for (putting a scene, where I am compelled h\ duty to praise men whom virtue commands nie to hate. When I arrive at my home, what aspect shall I assume, what

language shall I hold? His country lost, a good citizen ought to die. Had I but one man to destroy, in order to deliver my countrymen, I should turn to the task in one instant, and avenge my country and its violated laws by plunging my steel into the tyrant's bosoin. Life is a burden to me, because I enjoy no pleasure, and because all is pain to nie ; it is a burden, because the men with whom I live, and probably shall always live, have manners as widely different from mine as the moon's light differs from that of the sun. I cannot follow the sole mode of life which

S- T', & R 01) ft ft t could make it endurable, and a disgust for all is the consequence.' This passage affords a remarkable proof of the high-reaching sentiments which, even at the og> of seventeen, characterised Napoleon. The death which he meditates is the death of C'ato, not of Chatterton. It is not the pressure of penury which disgusts the extraordinary boy with life, but > he slavery of bis country and the degradation of his species. There is ample evidence existing among his early papers to prove, that lie was iu his youth a genuine an ani lit lover of republican liberty, and that In disliked the French, fixing his whole thoughts on Corsica. As his mind became matured, however, he saw that Ci'vsie i was too insignificant in extent, and P« -sed resources too limited, to permit it la flourish independently amid states so much superior to it in power; and he turned to France, as affording full scope for the development of those great problems iu social government which occupied so much of his youthful attention. Among the thirty-eight bundles of papers consigned by Napoleon to Cardinal Fesch, one curious paper deserves to be briefly referred to. It is a Dialogue on Law, which proves how early his opinions had been formed on this as oil other points. He never was remarkable for sentiment, and, at he commencement of his dialogue, he s|>. a ;.s in tin- co .damnatory manner of the i oi . th i i . between the sexes : þÿ 'I ic ii i hv hurtful to society, and to i i . ihu s more harm than good, ppincss of men ; I believe,

ii i Ii in ui would be conferred by lien j i.i iig power which should extinguish it, and deliver men from its influence.' Not w ii li e uniting litis denunciation, he was beyond question devotedly attached in his life io at least one woman þÿ Josephine. His letters to her from Italy carry passion even to extravagance. The writer in the lit rue de» Deux Months, from whom we derive these notices of Napoleon's early serving, that ' every ihirig proves days, concludes by ob- him to have \ in p 1 1 ti <l, like other men of genius, w I humanity which ordains that mulling great can be accomplished without great efforts. In spite of his superior talents, he had studied long and carefully those subjects in which he afterwards shewed himself a master. During many years, lie never ceased to read and reflect on the most profound existing works. If lie displayed ideas so correct on legislation, finance, and social organisation, these ideas did not spring spontaneously from his brain. On the throne, he only reaped the fruits of the long labours of the poor lieuteiiani of artillery. He formed his character by the m ans suited for the developni'M ; ii ii i men þÿ by toil, solitude, uuiirance. The Revolu- "1; i j i' liiiu a vast and brilliant h , L .; w i. bout that revolution, he would ill have been distinguished, for characters like his seize on fortune, and make it serve them. Let it be no more said that chance elevated Napoleon. When, after seven years of retirement, lie appear-

ed for the first time on the stage of the world, he contained already all the germs of his future greatness. Nothing was fortuitous in his case. He struggled to rise, and left no occasion unused to make himself known. He himself, therefore, must no more be permitted to ascribe his elevation to fatality.' To these truths nothing can be added. Never was it more ltilly shewn than in the case of Napoleon þÿ that industry is the better part o f genius.

TUESDAY, 9tii AUGUST, 1859. þÿ þÿ Inter-Colonial Intelligence We copy from the Barbados West Indian the Programme of the Fetes to he celebrated on the Inauguration of the Statue of the Empress Josephine, at Martinique, on the 29th inst. The invitation of the Governor of that colony to the authorities and inhabitants of the neighbouring Islands will, it seems, he heartily responded to by most of the Islands. A good many merchants and others will, we understand, leave St. Thomas for the purpose of being present on the occasion. From the extract of a letter from Zanzibar, which we also copy from the West Indian, it appears, that the Emigration of Free Laborers from Africa is carried on as vigor-

ously as ever. We trust that the arrangements, which Mr. Newton has been commissioned to make with Regis & Co. of Marseille, will soon be effected ; and that w7e may not long be without the aid of those valuable labourers.
PROGRAMME OE FETES AT THE INAU- GURATION OF THE STATUE OF THE E M PR ESS JOS E Pill N E .

The solemn inauguration of the Statue erected by the inhabitants of Martinique, on the Place þÿd Armes of Fort do France, in honor of the Empress Josephine, born in this Colony, will take place on Monday 29th of August nest. On August 28th, at sunset, a salvo of 21 guns will be fired from the batteries of Fort St. Louis, and Fort Dcsaix at Fort do France, to announce the opening of the fetes. This salvo will be repeated the next day at sunrise, sunset, and at the time when the Statue is uncovered. At each salvo the Rand of the 1st Regiment of Marine Infantry will perform at the foot of the Statue, as also at the time of the Inauguration of the portraits of their Majesties the Emperor and Empress, during the Ploughing Match, and at t he distribution of premiums and medals, which will take place on the 29th, 30th. and 31st of August. The troops in Garrison and the seamen of the Port, the deputations from the Garrisons and forces of other places, will repair to the Place þÿd Amies, at 7 þÿo clock on the morning of the 29th. The Judicial, Administrative, and Military authorities, the Committee of Subscription and Inauguration of the Statue, the Jury of the Agtieultural Show, .and the poisons invited to the ceremony, will assemble at the Government Hou-c it 7 þÿo clock aud accompany the Governor to mass. the authoiit.es. After having uncovered the Statue and distributed the rewards to the successful exhibitors, the Governor will review the troops. RARBADOS. A young countryman of ours, writing to his relatives in Barbados from Zanzibar, an Island on the East Coast of Africa, at the entrance of the Red Sea, (where do our countrymen not find their way ? ) says he formed one of a company entertained by the Sultan of Zanzibar at dinner, at which to their surprise, they were furnished not only with knives and forks, but with chairs to sit on þÿ quite a novelty in the East ; and the r. past, though not in the European style, tolerably good. At this out of the way place, as wo may term it, there were three or tour British Vessels of War, and one French þÿ amongst the former II M. Brig Persian, which was hero some few years ago. The Slave Trade was pursued quite vigorously ; and recently a French Bark bad appeared in the road with a cargo of 300 slaves, whilst II M. Brig Lynx was lying there ; but the Lynx could not interfere, because of a Charter which the Bark had to hire Laborers for the French Colony of Reunion. According to appearances, the French were encouraging a revival of the Slave Trade in those parts, under the pretence of Free Immigration. Another of II. M. Ships, the Lyra, had captured not less than 1C slaves within a few months previously. They were vessels of native build, navigated by and belonging to natives along the coast, who carry on the Slave Trade, supplying formerly the East with slaves. þÿ West Indian.

TRINIDAD. SUMMARY FOR THE þÿPACKET . The most startling piece of intelligence afforded by the history of the past fortnight, is the record of an attempt at a crime which hero is as rare as it is dastardly and flagitious. The news of the shootings lately occurring in Bar- I bados seems to have excited an imitative emulation amongst some here : and when it is renumbered now our population is constituted, comprising the drainings from the whole of the other islands, it would scarcely be a matter of surprise if we found all the woist traits of the lowest grades in all the other islands displayed here with increased effect. Our gaol returns and the every-day experience of the police courts, show how much greater the proportion of the crime of tlio country is committed by fresh imports from the other islands, one or two of which have quite an unenviable notoriety sending for hither the dregs of their pothe sons of the soil that have to be consider- pulation. It is not þÿ ed when crimes, disturbances, and discontents are thought of, but that medly of every grade which we receive, and receive gladly from elscwhere. The night of Wednesday, the 23rd, will be remembered in Trinidad as affording t lie first instance of a crime analogous in nature to tho deeds for which þÿIreland tenantry s have become famous assassination, fortunately þÿ in this ease only attempted þÿ in revenge for the discharge of public duties. One thousand dollars have been offered for information that may lead to the ap-

prehension ol tlio offender, but no certain clue lias yet been obtained. The Council of Government, on the first, were engaged in the consideration of a memorial from Merchants and others in the Port of Spain for extended time to land cargoes and a petition from Landing Waiters, on the other hand, to the Council to interpose to prevent their being called upon to work after hours. It seems probable that the question will be settled in the most reasonable way, either by tbc appointment of aid waters, or tho drawing up a scale of remuneration to be paid the tide waiters for working extra hours, by either of which means the consignees of Vessels may obtain, by payment of a slight fee, an occasional extension of the prescribed time. A despatch from tho Under Secretary of State | for the Colonies, Lord Carnarvon, sanctions provisionally the finacial arrangements þÿ made here for the introduction of Coolies 3,000 lately next season þÿ but impresses the doctrine that as the planters are tlig gainers by the immigration, they must chiefly bear the expense; and notices with some misgivings the increased duty on

Rum, as a tax which falls on the þÿconsumer that is on the inhabitants generally. Several measures were introduced or advanced a stage: one to authorise the Government to take up monies at the Colonial Bank in advance of revenue þÿ to obtain better interpreters from India þÿ to remit duty on goods imported for Tramroads þÿ to encourage steam communication with the Spanish Main ; the Ordinance to encourage the breeding of cattle and extension of pasture lands was read a third time and passed. The Venezuelan Government are before us in this particular, and every now and then wo are visited by one of the Steamers they liavo in service; the Apure was here the other day, and has returned. The state of the Vcnezuelean republic is so terribly unsettled now that commerce and all intercourse indeed are quite put a stop to. Several districts were by the latest advices in arms aginst the Government and Sotillo is still trying bard to maintain the Monagas cause. The district of the gold fields of Caratal is one of tliose disturbed, and the men employed in the diggings have been obliged to take to fighting. The detachment of white troops stationed here have beeu changed ; in place of the two companies of the list, we have now two of the 49th. Nothing lias lapsed as to the result of the investigations of Commission sent down to examine into the healthiness of the Barracks Tenders have been advertised for to build a new Town Hall in San Fernando. Competitors are invited to send in plans, and twenty live

dollars offered as a premium for tho best. The weather lias been most favorable to tbc growth of the sprouting canes ; every where the cane pieces are covered with verdure of the most promising aspect, but from the quantity of rain which has fallen, the roads arc rendered almost impassable tor mud, and the struggle to get down the last few canes, and get up the last few supplies, is a most arduous one. An invitation, couched in the most flattering terms, has, we learn, been received by Ilis Excellency tlio Creoles of Trinadau þÿ Mr. Breen. From the New York Herald. Peace and the NapoleonicPolicy in þÿEurope Whose Turn Conies Next? The peace which Louis Napoleon lias so suddenly arrauged with Austria is characteristic of the man, and is evidently a part of the same policy which governed him in closing the Crimean war, and which he laid down twenty yeais ago in his essay on the Napoleonic ideas. As with the proposition for the armistice, so, we doubt not, the terms of the peace all emanated from him. After the successive defeats he had experienced on the field of battle, the young Emperor of Austria was in no frame of mind to proffer terms of arrangement, or to hope for such moderate conditions as those he has obtained. Louis Napoleon, on the other hand, was not only able to offer them without a shade of dishonor, but it was an important part of his policy to prove to Europe the moderation of his demands. Die moral victory he has obtained in this respect over the doubts of united Europe is worth more to his policy and dyDasty than the conquest of Venctia ten times over could have been The clu ers that went up from the benches of the Briiish House of Commons when the despatch was read announcing that peace had been made, prove how well he understands the tone and temper of Europe, and how skilfully he plays upon them. Those cheers constitute the true ratification of his Italian policy, for England will not now oppose it, and no other Power will dare to do so. Let us now see what, this Italian policy is. Lombardy is torn from Austria, aud goes to

swell the power of Sardinia, now more than ever the fief of Franco. An Italian Confederation is formed, with the Pope at its head. Thu þÿPope c s onsent to this was not asked ; Naples was not invited; the wishes of the petty duros of Tuscany, Parma aDd Modena were not consulted : the plan was concocted by Louis Napo leou, perhaps with the assistance of Victor Emanuel and Count Cavour; and Francis Joseph comes into it as King ofVeuetia. These three being agreed, the others must cousent, whether they will or no, and the policy that will rule in their counsels is the Napoleonic policy. Should the Pope not consent, Louts Napoleon has only to withdraw his troops from Rome, and the Romans will soon bring him to reason. With the Napoleonic ideas ruling in Italy, the first thing the Pope must do is to discharge all his clerical ministers, and administer the Confederafon through a cabinet of laymen. It is not bable that Louis Napoleon would consent fo pro- any other course, nor Victor Emanuel, who ha driven the monks and Jesuits from his domain. A little time will be required to consolidate this scheme, but it stands from this time forth, and

adds aDotber country to the list where Napoleonic ideas prevail. Thus will they go on conquering Europe, and every new advance augments the moral power ot France and diminishes the weight and unity ot antagonism to them Like a skilful workman, Louis Napoleon stops at every new step, and allows time to cement his alliauces and secure his friendships. this peace, on Austria and the rest o! particularly The effect of this war, and more Germany, Will be remarkable. It will drive some sense and not a few new ideas into the thick-skulled Germans In Austria it may produce an entire change of policy on the part of the government, and enable it to reconstruct its motley empire in accordance with the ideas of the age. The Crimean war killed the old ideas in Russia, emancipated the serfs, imbued it with the commercial spirit of Western Europe, lined its plains with railroads, and opened its rivers to steam navigation. The developemeut of these things will of itself beget further political and industrial revolutions there. So it will be with Austria. Her young Emperor, seeing the folly of resistance, and induced with the new ideas, which required the cannon of Montebello, Magenta and Solforino to impress them upon the Austriau Court, is very likely to follow the example of Alexander II., and take kindly the inoculation of the Napoleonic ideas. There is, perhaps, another reason why he should do so. When he wout into the present struggle, he counted as strongly on the assistance of the

rest of Germany as Russsia did on that of Austria for the war in the Crimea. Russia has now been paying Austria for her course then, and Austria will yet have an opportunity to pay Prussia and the other German States for their course now. As soon as the. rule of the Napoleonic policy is consolidated in Italy, the Emperor ot the French will fiud a reason for quarrelling with some of the German States on the Rhine. þÿI lie question now is, whose turn comes next ? Louis Napoleon has told the world years ago that his foreign policy is to pick his quarrels one by one, and not to have all the Powers on hintself at once. What next, then ? Spain long since admitted the Napoleonic ideas without the strife of arms. Russia had to be inoculated with the bayonet, but has taken the infection very kindly. They henceforth tule in Italy, and Austria will not again opeuly resist, if she does not advocate them. There remains, then, of the great Powers, only Germany and England. No doubt Germany will next be taken in band. Racked by t lie moral consent and physical quietude of Russia, Spain, Austria and Italy, Franco can easily find cause of quarrel with some of the small German States, and then push her frontier to the Rhine Prussia, Bavaria and llanover have yet to swallow their recent big words and haughty menaces. The forty petty princes ruling in Germany now resist the Napoleonic ideas, and they must be knocked into their thick heads amid the din of battle. This will he done, and then will come the

turn of England. Some may think this an error þÿ that the people of England are already more than imbued with the commercial and progressive ideas of the Napoleonic policy, aud that the cheers of a Rritish House of Commons for a French Emperor will save England. We admit this in regard to the Rritish people. But their rule in the government is neither secure nor stable. The old Court and aristocratic party in England entertain very different views, and they arc a constant menace to the rule of the Napoleonic ideas on the Continent. They cling to the old ideas of George the Third, and may at any time adopt and endeavor to carry out his policy of a coalition of nil the nations against France. As long as this danger stands the Napoleonic policy is not safe. It must be removed, and for this is Cherbourg, and the mighty navy France is creating, and the Napoleonic coalition Louis Napoleon is gradually cementing on the Continent of Europe.

Trial of the Life-Preserving Stateroom. The trial of this invention, which took place at the Battery yesterday afternoon, drew together a large crowd, among whom we noticed several shipowners, captains of steamers, and other nautical persons. The float on which the stateroom was placed was loaded heavily with chain cables, the room being covered with light woodwork, corresponding to the hurricane-deck of a steamer. At 3J þÿo clock six poisons entered the siat. room, one of whom was Mr. Smith, the proprietor; the others were Capt. King, formerly ot the steamship Washington, Theodore Payne, who was one of the saved from the wreck of the Central America, Dr. Jones, of the Scientific American, R. H. Tarbell, Esq., and a reporter of the Times. Everything being ready, the door was shut and secured by screws upon the inside. A large opening at the top, aud a common sideport being left open to admit air. Mr. Hallack, the inventor, then opened the bottom valve, which, in a few moments, filled the float, and begun to sink. As the float went down, the state-room, which has a sustaining power of five or six tons, floated, carrying oil tlie light deck overhead, and swung clear of the imaginary wreck. At this instant an enthusiastic poi son from within thankful no doubt for his preservation, showed his head through the hatchway, and, displaying a small American flag, called for three cheers on the new life preserving invention The stateroom was kept in an upright position by the water secured in tanks at the bottom, and bad no moro

motion than an ordinary boat. There was space for twice the number that occupied tho rooms, aud they moved about, sat still, or climbed Upon the outside as they felt inclined. Alter being towed about for some time, it was brought back and secured. Those who went into the stateroom expressed entire satisfaction with the experiment, and Capt. King, who has a life experience upon the ocean, says it would float with entire safety in the roughest sea. Placed upon pai-genger steamers, it would, it is claimed, afford perfect security to the passengers in ease of sudden collision or other accident, and would also furnish the means ol preserving the specie and mails. It is provided with an illuminating apparatus for use at night, to attract the notice of passing vessels, and drifters or rudders worked from the inside, by which its motions can be directed, and which will serve as props when it is cast upon the shore. þÿ he I proprietors have secured European as well as American þÿpatents. CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 2nd SEPTEMBER, 1S59. The Royal Mail Steam Packet Shannon arrived at St. Thomas on Wednesday, having accomplished the voyage out in thirteen days. The Conference of Zurich met on the 6th August. It is confidently expected that the whole matter of revising the treaty of peace will be accomplished in a few sittings. The Great Eastern is now completed and will probably proceed to sea in the present month. It is hardly yet settled where the first experimental trip will extend to ; but it is supposed that the ship will first proceed some three or four hundred miles out to sea and return ; that on her return she will steam down to Portland, and, if the weather should be fine, cross over to Cherbourg. Ultimately her destination is to be Portland, in the United States.
