THE ITALIAN DUCHIES. ( From the Times' Correspondent. Modena, August 7. We have now a railway in Central Italy, from Piacenza to Bologna, and die first use tbe people of these countries have put their railway to has been a series of friendly þÿfraternizing visits. Last Sunday the people of Modena, Reggio, Parma. Bohigna, &c., met at a friendly banquet at To-day the rendezvous is at Piacenza. A fortnight ago it. took place at Modena, ipe. The people of Central Italy feel the want of holding together, and these otherwise idle solemnities have the good effect of bringing into contact kindred races, whom the jealousy of despotism had hitherto by main force kept asunder. But the railway is also used for more important purposes. Ail militant Italy is hurrying over to these central provinces. No train moves eastward without conveying hundreds of discharged volunteers from Lombardy aud Piedmont to all the towns of the ./Emilia, and especially to Modena. The Dictator Farini has assembled a large force under bis orders. Modena and Tuscany have signed an offensive and defensive league ; and tbe 12,000 men of tbe Tueoao division, on thsir way book from Lombardy, were directed to take up their quarters defended bj- i n s rvo ot 3,000 men aud only in this place. The Grand Duchy itself is the National Gna <1 Besides the 12,0U0 Tuscans aud their fi»e ill a-nalf batteries, Fariui has organized a Mod :,a B ig.ui, , 6,000 men strong, chiefly rec.uned among the discharged volunteeis from the Piedmontese regimeuts. An-

other brigade, also ot 6,OOo men, is to be in a few days, beaiing tbe name of Brigata ready Reggio The whole National Guard of the Duchy from the age of 18 to 35 Las been mobilized. In the Romagna, on the other hand, Mezzocapo their vanguard is at Rimini, and protects the ; and Rosselli are at the head of 12,000 men narrow pass of La Cattolica. 6,000 Tuscaus guard the Eodeneso frontier on the side of Mantua, with their head-quarters at the Ducal stronghold of Brescello. Tuscany and Modena constitute but one military Power. Farini has secured the services of General Fanti, a Moncncse, who so sigually distinguished himself at the late campaign. Cialdiui, a native of during the head of a Piedmontese corps d'armee Reggio, is also expected. Garibaldi is to bring bis Cacciatori delle Alpi to Central Italy, and to take the command of a vast body of volunteers. The Generals under Fanti at Modena are Ulloa, the leader of the Tuscan army, aud Kibotli, the commander of the Cassiatori della Alogra. To support this vast armament the fuuds, it seems, are forthcoming. The loan of 2,300,000f. opened by Farini has been promptly filled up by the comuni, or townships of the Duchy. The Dictator, who has already put the very considerable domains of the banished Duke under sequestration, is now contemplating the sale of tbe broad lands belonging to the expelled Jesuits. This Dictator, this Fariui, not one of the most amiable, accomplished, and polished men in Italy, has been seized by a fit of enthu-

siasm, which proves contagions to all who approach him, and which seems to have called forth all the latent energies of his nature. He saw yesterday, lor an hour, Couut lleiset, as he went past Modena, at the railway station. He informed the astouuded Imperial Envoy that both he (Farini) aud his people were in terrible earnest. He made the Couut understand that between him aud the Modenese there was a

, bond of life and death ; that he would have the town battered down, burnt, and levelled with the ground, and tbe country laid waste and strewn with salt, sooner than lie would see the Duke restored either by bis own or by other forces. You must remember that Farini is an old friend of tho Bonaparte family, having beeu a doctor in tbe family of' King þÿJoseph Although I have no doubt he would carry matters to the greatest extremities, were he hard driven, I am also inclined to think lie has, to some extent, the warrant of the French Emperor for bis present remarkably energetic conduct. The Emperor evidently wants to back out of tbe promise made to the Austrian Monarch at Villafrauea with respect to the restoration of tbe Dukes of Modena aud Tuscany. He is fain to raise up such au opposition in the country as may entitle him to declare such a restoration au impossibility. þÿ He will have no riots or disturþÿbances, he says, þÿ buthe wishes the people to speak out their minds as loudly as they can þÿmauage. Farini and the other rulors of Central Italy, mistrusting the lukewarmness and faintheartedness of the Moderate Party, have called the Reds to their assistance. The Minister of War at Modena is Colonel Frapolli, one of the most distinguished men who were at the defence of Romo under Ma/.zini. Nicola Fabriei, of Modena, also a Mazzinian, but a rightminded patriot, is now playing a conspicuous part here. Fariui aud the other leaders of this Central Italian movement are sure the þÿ þÿReds

are only Republicans when they despair of their country under any other forms, and feel sure of their ability to keep them under control. For the rest, at the present day they are all loudly calling for that Ceutral Italian Kingdom which is now in contemplation which is favourably looked upon by Napoleon III , to which Tuscauy and Modena, and in all probability Parma also, will belong, and tbe crown of which seems destined to gird the brow of the young heir of the Duchess of Parma. The destinies of the Romagna are less certain; but Napoleon III. encourages the hopes of the people of the Legations for an independent State, only bound to the Pope by tbe flimsiest ties of suzerainetc, aud acknowledging such supremacy by tbe payment ot a trifling tribute Such arc the prospects of these revolutionized provinces at the present moment, and I can readily believe that the actual preoccupation and tension of men's minds are so great and general that they have no leisure and no fancy for their daily occupation. All business is at a standstill, so that the statistics of crime itself present a most astonishing decrease. Popular excitement has certainly been wound up to its highest pitch by the declaration of the Emperor Napoleon that þÿ he, for one, would never be the man to effect tbe restoration of any Italian Sovereign by force of þÿarms, It seems very easy to infer that if be will not venture on aimed intervention, neither will he suffer the Austrians to take up the quarrel of their aiicieut

allies sword in hand. Without the armed interference of either Franco or Austria, the return ol the exiled Princes seems to every sane man a most impracticable undertaking. The Italians, however, are not merely arming against such forces as either their Princes or their Swiss mercenaries, or their Spanish and Neapolitan auxiliaries, may bring against them. If Napoleon III play false, and the worst come to the worst, they vow to hold their own even against Austria and France. Farini is prepared to lay Modena in ashes. Bologna proposes to renew the prodigies ot valour of tho siege of Rome in 1849.

PRUSSIA. (From the þÿTimes Correspondent.) Berlin, August 10. I he attention of politicians here is naturally called to tho Congress which is expected ter follow the Zurich Conference. While Austria still seems to hesitate, Prussia is not averse from tho proposal, on condition that the Italian Confederation shall become a fact. She will then support tho restoration of the banished Princes to their dukedoms, but only on the condition of their granting constitutions and extensive administrative reforms. Prussia is perfectly sincere in this, as it proved by the King of þÿNaples conditional s assent to join the Confederation, which was given after consulting tho Prince Regent.

The Conference of Zurich is likely to be, in ! its way, as great a surprise for the worbl in geuei ul as the armistice or the peace of Villafranc i It is understood here that, instead of mak ii all the difficulties which were expected, Aust i, having consulted some ot those female divinities whose worship she so wisely prefers to iiat of roystering Mars, is prepared to make at once the concession which will secure a speedy conclusion of the treaty. To her only two points are of importance þÿ the restoration ot the Dukes and the establishment of the Confederation. If she brings these about, she will have acquired in the face of Europe all that she ever aimed at, and more than she gaioed by the separate treaties. Ouce more her defeat will have been a victory. She has had long practice in managing a Confederation, and rather likes the amusement. I have mentioned the general call for a reform of the Diet. It has been heard even in Vienua, and it is said that the Ministers there, having nothing to do at home, are employing their abundaut leisure in concocting a refoim of the federal constitution. I believe that when it appears it will turn out to be a rifacciamento of the reform planned at Dreslen in the winter of 18.30-1, which was only not adopted in consequence of the determined opposition of the smaller States. As far as Prussia was concerned, M. von Munteuffcl had uothiug to say again-t the plan. He had before declared that the only institution wanting in Germany was a

political exiinguishcr or lire brigade. The Berliners hailed the invention as the wished-for extinguisher, hut, though deserted by Prussia, the smaller States saved themselves. Only Austiia appreciated the value of the þÿ precious þÿmaterials which the plan offered, and is now preparing a second edition, with some slight varnish ot liberalism to make it look new. Its effect would have been to create a great police union, to increase the power of the middle States, Saxony, Hanover, Bavaria, and Wurtemberg, to subjugate the smaller Princes, and to annihilate such influence as Prussia has hitherto possessed. Austria is ready to prove her readine ss to join in, and even to propose, reforms of this nature. Ouc of the first propositions to bo brought forward in the next Diet will be the. fortification of the north and north-east coasts. If, as is not improbable, the proposition he rejected, then Prussia will carry out the plan in conjunction with the seaboard States. Up to the present time the coasts of Germany have been entirely defenceless, for it has always been taken as an axiom that there was nothing to fear from England, and that the English Government would never suffer a French fleet to sail through the Channel with þÿhos ile intentions. Now, however, that Count Wa)ew6ki has stated to a diplomatist in Paris that, as far as the English Ministers wore concerned, the French fleet was as free to act in the German Ocean or the Baltic as in the Adriatic, the matter has assumed a different complexion. We, who

have just discovered that our own coasts are exposed to possible attacks, cannot find fault with the North Germans if they leel alarmed at seeing their theory of our naval supremacy and its consequences suddenly overturned. People, are only now beginning to appreciate the ifl'ect of our intimate alliance with France, and tiic change this has made in the conditions of the European equilibrium.

THE PAPAL STATES. BoLOtiNA, Altg, 8. The people of the Legations, as well as their rulers, seem to me less sanguine in their hopes for the ultimate success of their cause than the Modenese population and their intrepid Dictator, Farini. A letter of the Emperor Napoleon III. to the Duke of Gramont, in Rome, is sold under the porticoes of Bologna. It can be no news iu England, as I already had lull knowledge of it in Turin five days ago ; but it is read with great eagerness hero as a notable piece of news. The Emperor þÿ has promised to maintain inviolate the sovereignty of the Pontiff in þÿRome. He can þÿ neither acknowledge nor sanction the deed by which the Legations separated themselves from þÿRome; hut he thinks þÿ he has 1 neither the right nor the duty to meddle with the internal affairs of the þÿLegations.

f « Q i Qj Q X toil & $ This lends itself to an endless variety of constructions. The most sober patriots there, however, must needs conjecture that the Emperor means to secure to the Pope the sovereignty of the Legations, but also to bestow on these provinces the blessing of a separate lay administration. Not a lew imagine that the Legations will have nothing in common with the rest of the State except only the person of the Sovereign ; that this fairest and wealthiest divisiou of the Papal States will be united to the rest on about the same terms as those which joiu Norway to Sweden ; so that even legislative independence shall he completely secured, and the Pope will only personally or vicariously preside over their legislative assemblies. But others, again, remeniheriug how the separation of the Legations from the domains of the Papal see was twice carried out by the first Napoleon, and with the explicit, however reluctant consent of two successive Popes, so that these provinces, both as part of the Cisalpine Republic aud of the kingdom of Italy, were emancipated from priestly rule for 20 yeais (1796) þÿ 1814J, Hatter themselves that the Pope may he induced ouce more to sanction such a separation that the Legations may be auuexed to Piedmont and the State of aud the State of Central Italy, aud that all Northern Italy, þÿ or, otherwise, to Tuscany þÿ the Pope will contend lor will be a tribute in money, to be paid by the severed provinces þÿ a tribute which, after a short lapse of time,

would become as obsolete as the gift of the Chinea, or white ambling palfrey laden with gold and jewels, tvlrieh is due to His Holiuess by that pious vassal the King ot the Two Sicilies, aud against the non-payment of which the Pope annually protests, although the protest never did him any shadow of good. In order that some even of the most moderate hopes, and, as Napoleon III. says, þÿ of had arrived a lew the most legitimate þÿvows of the patriots of these provinces may Le realized, it is universally felt here that the countiy must arm, and this is now the sole business of the entire population. A couple of Piedmontese battalions are still in Bologna, hut they leave this day or tomorrow at the latest. The Piedmontese uniform, however, meets us at every step, as the volunteers of Romagna have been clad after the strictest Sardinian pattern. There aro 8,000 well-armed and equipped meu under General Mcz/.acapo, with two batteries of eight guns each. Hosselli is at the head of 3,000 more combatants, all natives of the Legations. Only two battalions of the National Guard are now mobilized, fully clad, and iu perfectly warlike trim ; hut I am assured that in less than a fortnight 16 such battalions will he forthcoming. Mezzacapo, with 6,000 of his chosen troops, has his head-quarters ut Forli, while strong battalions arc echelonned at Geseua, Rtrniui, &c , as far as the defile ot La (Jattolica. On the side of þÿ1 erugia aud Citta de Castello no attack is expected, as the Apeunine Passes iu

those several directions are arduous aud rugged, and the roads impracticable, at least for artillery. In reality, the people of this country deem themselves aud are perfectly sale from any onset on the part of the Papal troops, whether Swiss or natives, aud laugh to scorn all idea of any aid His Holiness may receive either from Naples or Spain. They think their accounts must be settled with France aud Aus- | tria; they are ready to submit to the ultimate fiat of the former Power, but they do not shrink from a desperate conflict with all tho might of the latter. As at Parma and Modena every door at Bologna aud throughuut Romagna heais nostro legUlimo lie the inscription, þÿ Viva Vittorio Rmmanuele, or þÿ Vogltamo Vittorio Emmanuele per nostro Re." The most sensible persons, however, have but little hope of joining Piedmont and Lombardy, and they begin to look to a formation of a kingdom of Central Italy consisting Tuscany, of the Duchies, and the Legations, as the most plausible solution of the preseut political knot. They think they may receive from England great a deal of help and support ii such a plan is ever laid before a European Congress ; they flatter themselves that tho Protestant Powers which allowed the Pope to be propped up by French and Austrian bayonets in 1849 may now find out that they have an interest in insisting that lie should rely for existence on bis own unaided resources.

MASSACRE OF EUROPEANS IN BORNEO. The China Telegraph contains tho following account of the massacre at Baujei massing, on the south coast of Borneo, a brief notice of which has already appeared : þÿ þÿ It appears that for some time past great discontent existed among the natives at the election of the new Sultan, who was not the lineal descendant of their late ruler, hut had been adopted by him as a son ; and a conspiracy was formed to depose him, unknown to the Dutch Resident, Count Beutheim Fecklenburgh llheds. At the head of a conspiracy was a certain Aling, a native of Muning, who aspired to the sovereignty of Bajerinassing, calling himself, in his proclamations, by the style and title of Radja Kuuing. On the breaking out of the conspiracy, a general massacre of the Europeans was to take place. The Hag of the conspirators was unfurled on May 1, aud the European workmen employed in the coal mines of Julia llermina, belonging to a joint-stock company, aud situated near Kalangan, were suddenly attacked, overpowered, and brutally murdered, with the exception of two or three women, who managed to conceal themselves with their children. An attack was then made on tho establishment at Paugeran, but the assailants had to draw oft' with some loss, having met with a very warm reception. In other parts of the island the massacre of the Europeans was general aud simultaneous. Amongst the unfortunate victims of this brutal and wholesale murder are five German missionaries (Messrs. Hammer, llott,

Wiegand, Kind, and Hufmeister), with their wives aud children. Tho total number of Europeans muidered and missing is between 70 aud 80. Mobt providentially, Colonel Andrcson days previously (April 28) with a detachment of 150 meu of the 9th battalion, to relievo Count Benjamin ot the civil government as resident, aud to take the military command of tho station. This probably preserved Tatus, the chief town of Banjermassiug, 1'roiti a similar horrible fate ; hut a party of 50 men, sent for the protection of þÿI angcian, were intercepted by a strong hand of rebels, and obliged to return. Orders were immediately after dispatched by tho resident to send over the other five companies of the 9th battalion, some artillery, aud half a company of Sappers, by tho Dutch war-stcamcrs Moutrado aud Ardjuno, to Banjerinassing, as a reinforcement and protection. Later accounts hud been received from þÿl angeran,stating that the little band of Europeans shut up there were defending themselves most heroically, and had successfully withstood and driven back tho assail ants ten different times. Great complaints had been made against the Government, or at least against the Resident, for not affording tho workmen of the coal mining company tho protection they were promised by their charter; and tho Governor-General had ordered an official investigation to be made, with a view of ascertaining whether these charges had auy foundation. The following also were among the victims of this cold-blooded outrage : þÿ Mr.
Wijumalen and family (except the three youngest children), Mr. and Mrs. Motley ami child (English), l)r. Hinzenger, Messrs. Van Ilercken, Eisenger aud Brood.

The success of the ship-lifting apparatus at tho Victoria Docks has induced Messrs. Brunlees aud Webb to propose that the problem regarding the Suez passage should he solved by the abandonment of tho canal scheme and the construction of a ship railway between the two seas. According to their views piers of piling would be erected at each port, vessels would bo lifted and lowered by hydraulic power, tho transit would be effected in cradles resting on five lines of railway, any one of which would be available for ordinary traffic, and a speed of 20 miles an hour could he anticipated The estimated cost would bo 1,800, 000/. agamst the 6,400,000/. demanded by M. de Lesscps, which many engineers assert would be swollen to 30,000,000/. It is also pointed out that tho vessels while on their cradles could be examined or even repaired as if in graving docks, that their sails would be of better use on tlio railway than on the canal, and that the constant cost of dredging and clearance would he wholly avoided.

THE SERF QUESTION IN RUSSIA- ('ROM the þÿtimes correspondent.) St. Petersburg, July 27. Serfdom in Russia is a modification, and a very slight one, of absolute slavery. The serf cannot be sold away from the estate on which lie was born, such estate being valued, Dot for the quantity of its acres, but for the number of serfs attached thereto. The master may not inflict capital punishment, and must provide his serfs with food and houses þÿ if the wretched hovels they inhabit arc worthy of that name. With these exceptions, the þÿmaster powers s are absolute. The serf cannot marry without his þÿlord sconsent, though early marriages are eucouraged, their produce being valuable. The owner can iuflict corporal punishment, give the serf any amount of labour, or lease his services to another master. During the reign of the late Emperor no attention was paid to the condition of the serf. For Imperial purposes he was simply so much food lor powder. Constant requisitions were made on the landowners for their due proportion of serfs to si rve iD the ranks ; generally at the rate of seven, eight, or ten per thousand. These requisitions were made in autumn, after the harvest, or iu early winter. The serf was sent at his þÿmaster s cost to the appointed depot for recruits, frequently at a considerable distance from the estate. Such was the desire to escape military service, and so great the mortality en route. Irom neglect, insufficient clothing, and bad food, that in order to secure the arrival of the required number at the depot half as

many more were despatched from the estate. On reaching the depot the serf was handed over to the barber and deprived of the mass of hair þÿ þÿnature s preservative against cough and catarrh þÿ in which his chin and throat had been enveloped from early manhood. His whisker was shaven close to the ear and he was sent to drill. \ are 50 or 60 daily, weekly, and monthly papers This naturally produced great mortality from pulmonary, throat, and chest disease. The survivors, being enlisted for 25 years, generally finished their career in the military service.

This promise has been strictly fulfilled, not a single recruit having been raised throughout Russia since the treaty of Paris was signed. Active, intelligent, and kind hearted, Alexander II. saw and felt how necessary it was to relieve bis empire from the stigma of slavery, aud how much more powerful he would become as the ruler of 60,000,000 freemen. Ho knew that his views would be opposed by the old Russian party, who maintain that Russia wants hands, not land, and declare that tire serfs once emancipated would soon become the masters. He therefore determined to proceed cautiously and slowly. Committees were organized in every province of the empire for the purpose of considering the question in all its bearing.-. At the head of the central committee the Emperor placed Count Orloff, the leader of the old Russian party, and whoso name carries the greatest weight ainoDg them. Though the Count probably disapproved the Imperial plans, his opposition was thus silenced and his concurrence obtained. The largest proportion of members composing these committees was nominated by the proprietors, the remainder being appointed by the Government through the Governors General of the different provinces. The deter-
mination of the Emperor is, first, that in the course of 12 or 15 years serfdom shall be en-

tirely abolished, and the serf shall he a freeman ; secoudly, that the house in which he has been living and a small portion of land shall become his property, or that of a free community whereof lie is a member. This house and land are to be paid for either in labour or some other manner, and the committees are to report as to the best mode of arrangement. Not satisfied with the mere appointment of committees, the Emperor last year made a tour through a great portion of his dominions, and placed himself in direct communication with the landowners, encouraging the willing and rebuking the forward. The greater number of these committees havo aheady made their reports to head-quarters at St. Petersburg. They have also elected sub-committees to proceed to the capital, where they will form one grand general committee, whose duty it will be to consider the reports aud decide on some plan to be | laid before the Emperor. The committees are nearly unanimous iu admitting the feasibility of the question submitted them, hut great difficulties have been raised as to the proposition to endow the serf with his bouse and land. Some suggest that the serf on each estate shall be placed in a village to be formed at one corner of the property, their houses being transported there, or wood given to them for buildiug new ones. Others contend that the serf should be set entirely free without land or house. The ground for these objections consists in the fact that an immense number of serfs reside in the

immediate vicinity of the þÿlandowners chateaux. If each of these becomes the owner of his house and land, the lords declare they will become prisoners in their castles, and will cease to be owners of their estates. The Government replies that if the serf be freed without house or land he will starve before obtaining employment, and it fears that if the masters he permitted to fix the sites for the proposed villages the emancipated serfs will be but ill lodged. Meanwhile, the papers daily report the speeches made by the members of the various committees at the close of their labours, on which they comment in very fair style. The war proved a great civiliser for many of the serfs. The blockade threw out of employment an immense number of labourers at St. Petersburg, whose curiosity became excited as to the events of the day. Those who had received some education spent their mornings in reading bulletins, &c.( to their fellow-workmen. At the various pot-houses near the mills the landlords gave refreshment gratis to those officials who would read the papers aloud, so as to attract customers. The demand caused an increase in the supply, and at this moment there

published at St. Petersburg, three-quarters of of which are writteu in Russian, and by far the greater portion started since the war. The most reliable information aud the most free dis- No sooner was the present Emperor relieved j cussiou are to he found in the Russian rather than in the French or German papers. The Government seems anxious that the internal condition of the empire should be fully discussed at home, without permitting the rest of Europe to take part in the debate. Russian local papers are also to be found throughout the eut ire empire ; indeed, there is hardly a government without one. In the St. Petersburg papers we find pretty fair reports of the proceedings in the English Parliament, translations of articles from The Times, accounts of the late war in Paly, comments on home and foreign affairs, &e. 1 will give you a sample, and take the St. Peterbrughsky Vedomosty of Friday last, the 22d inst , from which I translate the following intelligence : þÿ þÿ Within the last few days reports of the committees for the improvement of the position of the seifs have been signed in the governments of Koursk, Olonctz, and Orenburg. In a letter to the editor of the Moskovsky Vedimotz, on the close of the labours of the first of thee committees, it is stated that every member, while giving his opinion on this important matter, always remembered that on him were imposed the duties both of a Christian and of a citizen, and that in recording his vote he was

bound to unite the principles which should govern him in both characters, without swerving to the right or to the left. At a dinner given at the close of the Olonetz Committee Mr. Zotnmcr, among other remarks observed, þÿ þÿ This excellent work (the liberation of the serfs) requires the impulse of a clear conscience as well as the strictest impartiality. But, however holy

may bo our motives, and however pure and wellintentioned our labours, yet they are subject to the judgment of others. The judgment of our Monarch, who has called upon us to fulfil his will and that of Providence does not alarm us. It will be a wise and a just judgment. He may discover imperfections natural to all the works of mortals, but he will find nothing contrary to conscience or to honour. A more important judgment is that of our own fraternity, which may be founded on their different views a id connexions þÿ Again, at the closing of the Orenburg Committee, the Civil Governor, Acting Councillor of State BaranofLky, bore witness that in their report a wish to maintain the establishment of the landowners was closely combined with ait endeavour to improve the condition of the peasants in every respect þÿ The same paper contains a copy of a letter written to the Samarsky Goubernsky Vedomosty by Leonty Turgoneff, a member of the committee. From the N, Y. Weekly Tribune, July 23, 1859. SALIENT FEATURES OF THE WAR. Europe has rarely seen war on so gigantic a scale as that raging in Italy The campaigns of Conde and of Marlborough were far less imposing. The armies of the Great Frederick dwindle by the side of those that recently fought on the Mincio. In the variety and magnitude of their horrid enginery, and in the pomp and circumstance that surround them, they rival the colossal displays of the first Napoleon. This war has peculiarities that widely distinguish it from its predecessors. Though abounding in strange features, picturesque incidents and grand results, that in which it most impresses reflecting observers is the changes wrought by science and time, since the battle of Waterloo, in the materials of great armies, and iu the mode of wielding them during a protracted campaign. We will group together some of the more noteworthy of these, premising that they are novel only in their application to war, being quite common-place in other relations Among the more obvious of these changes is the transportation of troops and warlike material by steam power. The French army of 1795-6 marched to Italy, weary and foot-sore, around the spurs of the Maritime Alps. That of 1800, following the track of Hannibal, scaled by painful steps the Great St. Bernard, aud descended upon the plains through the gorges of the mountains But hardly had Europe heard that negotiations between Louis Napoleon and Francis Joseph were suspended, and that the Austrians had crossed the Ticino, when

Napoleon, by long processions of railway trains, poured masses of men and materials into the ports on the Mediterranean, whence fleets of steamers bore them swiftly to the Italian coast. Here railways distributed them to the points threatened by the Austrians. It was steam that prevented Francis Joseph gaining any advantage over the Allies by his precipitate advance into Sardinia. Montebello and Magenta witnessed an unprecedented application of steam power to the exigencies of battle. In the heat of the fight, railway trains brought to the ground a succession of re-enforcements from distant posts. The shrill whistlo of the locomotive, demanding a clear track as it arrived and departed, mingled with the clangor of the trumpets, the shouts of the combatants, and the booming of the cannon. And when the bloody strife had ebbed away, railway coaches bore the wounded and the dying off the field, to find a hospital or a grave. The same tireless agent has carried to the Mincio the heavy siege train to be used in battering the walls of Mantua. It has also deposited on the banks of that river, gun-boats iu fragments, to be there put together, and manned by amphibious troops from the harbors of France, to aid in reducing the fortress that so long defied the first Bonaparte. It was the steamer and the railway that enabled and emboldened the Emperor of the upon the impregnable þÿquadrangle, where the I rench to advance so rapidly and " fearlessly whole Austrian forces were posted ; for these

young servitors of old Mars could bring up fresh men, munitions and supplies even I aster than the Austrians could retreat or the Allies pursue. How different the result of the Russian invasion if the great Emperor had been foil .wed from Paris to Moscow by a friendly line of railway ! Hardly less useful to both armies is that other modern invention, the telegraph. Manipulated by the respective chiefs of the forces, distant troops, in the twinkling of an eye, receive orders to concentrate here, or strike a blow yonder, or move thither, which, in any previous European contest, it would have required days or weeks to communicate. Through the same medium, the two Emperors are now, doubtless, summoning re-enforcements from tbeir dominions for another, and perhaps another, great struggle, during the present Summer, which, but for the cooperating agencies of steam and electricity, would bs necessarily postponed to another campaign But it is in the instantaneous communication to the capitals of the belligerents, and thence to the world, of intelligence of important strategic movements and the result of great battles, that the changes wrought by science since Prance and her foes met in arms before, are most strikingly illnstrated After Napoleon I

Ilington and Blucher shook hands at La Belle Alliance over the victory of Waterloo, before Suine of the European capitals received authentic intelligence from that decisive field. At the end of sixty-three days meager accounts of the battle found their way into the metropolitan journals of America. So influential a newspaper as The Albany Gazette dismissed the subject iu four or five confused and unsatisfactory lines. During the first Napoleonic campaign iu Italy, nearly a month intei vened before F. ance knew that its stripling gcneial, iu three bloody conflicts, fought in just twice as many days, on and near the heights ul Ca-tiglione, had cut iu pieces three Autriau armies, led by three veteran commanders, killing, wounding and capturing 40,000 of the enemy. How marked the change now ! A great battle ebbs and flow- over the hills aud plains around Castiglioue, from early dawn till the going down of the sun As night slowly spreads its pail over the field, Paris illuminates its streets for the victory of Soiferino. While the Sardinian batteries, in the long eveniug of this bloody day, are still engaged in forcing back the stubborn Austrian rignt wing, half tnc capitals of Europe are bounding with joy over a field won, or drooping with regret for a battle lost. And in one week thereafter, this struggle

on the slopes of the Mincio is eagerly canvassed all along the western coast of the Atlantic aud on the shores of the Mexican Gulf, at the head waters of the St. Lawrence and at the mouth of the Mississippi, on hoard steamers floating on the great lakes and in log cabins on the banks of the Missouri 1 he homage paid to the press is one of the most gratifying peculiarities of this war. Even the monarch who gives warnings, imprisons editors, and silences journals in Paris, carries among the equipage of the Imperial camp a printing establishment, the symbol of liberty and progress. Leading European journals have correspondents with both armies, who give glowing pictures of the weary march, tire gay bivouac, and the terrible bai tie-shock Quite as trustworthy, and infinitely more graphic, than duced on both sides of the Ailantic, aud repro- the official dispatches, these pictures are read the world over This new feature ou the wrinkled front of Mars, e.-sentially democratic in its nature, is ot American origin. The idea is faintly traceable in the savans who accompanied Napoleon in the Egyptian campaign. But, systematic newspaper sketching of passing events in the camp and on the field was first practiced in our war with Mexico, was then timidly copied in the Crimea, aud is now the most attractive characteristic of the Italian campaign. rich materials lor the g.aver pen of the furnishing The.-e correspondents are bistoriau. Indeed, their warm descriptions are History þÿ a gallery living photographs of current events. ot

A rare incident of this eventful campaign is an attempted reconnaisance of the Austrian tion, just previous to the battle of Soiferino, posi- by means of a balloon ! Exact data concerning the whereabouts of your antagonist may decide the fate of an army or even an empire. VVe commend this subject to the attention of Messrs. Wise and La Mountain. And we commend them to Louis Napoleon, a-suring him that, in addition to their capacity for aeronautic reconnoitering, if they will assault the þÿenemy center s with halt as much vigor as they dashed iuto tho woods at the toot of Lake Ontario on thoir recent voyage, they will break the Austrian line more effectually tliau did Macdonald at Wagrutu or McMahon at Magenta. Seriously, though, this balloon experiment at Casteluedolo is another proof of the ingenuity and the French mind in everything versatility to war. pertaining of þÿ The recent improvements in weapons of war if that which makes them more deadly can be called an improvement þÿ of which so much is said, has hardly had the effect on the field that was anticipated. Cannon are doubtless more unerring in their aim, and carry shot longer distances, than at the beg uning of the century. The lighter guns are handled by skilful men and trained horses, with far greater celerity. The rifle can be fired five times as rapidly, can reach its mark with more certainty, and can kill at a fearfully long distance Pistols, of the Colt and

destructive weapon in close oombat. appallingly oognate stylea, have become an Infantry are unw trained to fence, thrust aud strike with the bayonet as unerringly and effectively as hussars ever did with their swords. And yet the slaughter at Montebello, Falestro, Magenta aud Soiferino would seem, judging from the imperfect returns, to fall much behind, in proportion to the numbers engaged, the great battles fought in Europe in the first fifteen years of this century. The London Times estimates tho combatants at Soiferino at 320,000 This is undoubtedly too small au estimate, but taking it for a basis, the number of killed and wounded, measured by the standard of Wagram, would be 57,000 ; measured by that of Jena, 83,000, and by that of Eylau, 122,000. We have seen no statement of the loss at Soiferino which readies even the lowest of these terrible figures- The accounts which place 50,000 hors du combat, fix the number engaged at 450,000 þÿ a loss less than two-thirds as great, proportionally, as that at Wagram, which was one of the least sanguinary of Napoleon's grand conflicts. One cause of this discrepancy is doubtless found in the fact þÿ not yet satisfactorily explained þÿ that in the Italian campaign victory has in no case been followed by one of those remorseless pursuits that usually marked the triumphs of the first Emperor, aiding to swell into gigantic proportions the heaps of dead and dying. But, though speculation on this point can, with the imperfect data yet received, only ap-

proximate to certainty ; enough is known to warrant the assertion, that the demon of war has not yet assumed so grim a visage on the plaiu of Italy as he used to wear when following the eagles of the elder Napoleon. Topics grow upon us, and we will mention but one more. Were an American to visit the French army in Italy, his attention would be arrested by the variety of troops of which it is composed. The Grenadiers and Voltigeurs of the Imperial Guard, the Chasseurs de Vincennes, the Turcos, the Zouaves, and other strangelyoostumed and uniquely-equipped corps, so like variegated and versatile France herself, would rivet his eye. And foremost among these would stand the world-renowned Zouaves. Composed of men of all classes, colors and climes, their half-Turkish, lialf-Moorish dress, and general Oriental mien and aspect, befit a corps which is a seeming cross between Don Cwsar De Bazan and Rob Roy, between a modern Alpine brigand and an ancient Knight of the Holy Sepulchre. Off duty, they are as gay and volatile as a Parisian ; but in tlie din of battle, as brave and bloody as a North American Indian or an Algerine corsair. They usually go through their evolutions on the run, and their favorite weapon is the cold steel of the bayonet. The world does not afford their match for hand toband street-fights ; to mount the walls of loopholed houses under a shower of rifle-halls, and clear them of the enemy ; to stand and be plowed by cannon shot till the tru mpet sounds the onset; to charge up to the mouth of a

spouting battery, or receive a galloping squadron of cavalry on their bayonet points ; to leap a moat or swim a river or scale a bill, in the face of a tempest of grape ; or to meet and master the most desperate exigencies that the bloody god can devise. At Palestro, we think it was, a battalion of them was ordered to silence a distant Austrian battery. As the trumpets sounded, they tore off their knapsacks, took the þÿ gymnastic þÿstep, which means a run, swam an intervening stream, holding their firearms high in air to keep their powder dry, dashed at the flamiog throats of the guns with the yell of Comanches, and, bounding clear over them, like BedouiD Arabs, firing one shot as they wui they transfixed half the gunners with their bayonets, and brained tho rest with the butts of their weapons. No Wonder the Austrian colonel who witnessed the sceoe said, þÿ These are not þÿmen they arc tigers þÿ! From Montebello to Soiferino, the Zouaves have left double their share of dead on every field, as testimonials that they pay with tbair þÿheart blood s for the title of þÿ the eraok þÿcorps of the French army.

From the Bermuda Royal Gazette of 30 th Aug. The Aurora Borealis.

This singular phenomenon made its appearance i in our Northern hemisphere on Sunday evening last. It appeared to ascend from a few degrees above the horizon towards the zenith, assuming a variety of shapes and beautiful colours þÿ sometimes in tremulous sheets of a pale yellow, changing gradually into a deep crimson, or shooting upwards in streams of light resembling those frequently observed from the setting sun. It covered at times the entire space between N. W. and N. E., leaving the sky, from the horizon to its apparent base, perfectly clear. Towards ten þÿo clock, it gradually died away, when the whole of the northern sky threw out a light resembling the pale light of the moon, which was sufficiently bright to cast a deep shadow from every object on the land. This light continued till dawn of day. þÿ The last time, we believe, that we were visited by the Northern twilight was in the year 1839. To the Editor of the Royal Gazette.

Sir, The unusual appearance of the Northern firmament on Sunday evening is worthy of a passing remark. The beautiful appearance of the sky, as it assumed the different phases presented to our view, reminded us of dissolving views exhibited by a Magic Lantern. First, there was a red glare as if thrown upward by a blazing ship; then this seemed mixed with gigantic stripes which melted into something like the beams shot forth by the rising sun ere it bursts in glory þÿo er our sleeping world : again this changed into the mellowing light of the Queenly moon, wading her nightly course in azure heaven ; and then, as if the east irradiated was by Sol, while the light of night held her sceptre þÿo er the far stretching North. Still other changes take place in this shifting scene, for the North West reflects a burning Vesuvius beautifully studded with glittering stars, and during all this time might be beheld great dark clouds shooting upwards between it and the sky, forming a striking contrast to the illuminated opaque above. Beautifully as the Aurora Borealis was hero seen on the occasion alluded to, it must have come far short of its glorious displays in the land of its birth. þÿ The co'.d icy þÿNorth. where the light it affords is of singular use to those who dwell in regions of eternal snow. The adaptation of this phenomena, to the exigencies of the human beings who reside near the pole, fully prove that þÿnature great s Architect had the welfare of our race in view when

He ord lined the fabric of the heavens, with all their glorious hosts of lights anil constellations, and is it possible that reasonable men can reflect on these things and not feel their minds elevated above the sordid trifles þÿo er which they pore on earth. Surely it becomes us when we behold such grand displays of creative beneficence to adore that being who has made absolutely nothing in heaven above or iu earth beneath without its specific use. þÿ Great and marvellous are thy works O God : in wisdom hast thou made them all þÿ Vours faithfully, REFLECTION. August 99, 1859

From the Neir York Herald. August þÿ 23.) ii i; \ i c: o. OUR SPECIAL WASHINGTON DESPATCH Washington, August 18, 1859. Professor Dimitry will sail for Punta Arenas via Aspiuwall and Pauama on the 5th September. His instructions are already prepared, lie will first secure the ratification of the Cass- Yrissari treaty, minus the clause obligating this government to suppress filibustering expeditions, if Jerez shall not have already accomplished that object, and then devote his efforts to the settlement of our claims by arbitration, the opening of the transit in accordance with existing contracts, and the negotiation of a liberal commercial treaty. It is the policy of the administration to establish permanent commercial relations with Central America, as the best method of American-

9 T « 9 ft P. II ft l| 9, izing that country. It is believed that the familiar acquaintance of Prof Dimitry with the language and manners, and sympathy with the religion of the people there, will greatly aid him in procuring such arrangements as are desired. Mexican affairs are daily assuming a more favorable aspect. The presence of Senor Lerdo here, in conjunction with Senor Mata, has alteady had a good effect. They had an interview with the President yesterday, and Gen. Cass to-day, which gave them much satisfaction. The success attending their negotiations for money and munitions has given the administration increased confidence in the ability of Juarez to carry on his government to permanent establishment. Every assistance consistent with the policy of our government will be accorded to Juarez. Senor Lerdo, accompanied by Senor Mata, has had a full and free conversation with the President on the subject of Mexican affairs. It is represented that the interview was mutually gratifying and instructive. Senor Lerdo will remain in the country for several weeks. General Cass called at the Mexican Legation ! to-day, aud paid his respects to Senors Lerdo and Mata, the former of whom is quite ill. Mr. McLane is looked for here early in September, with a treaty betweeu the Juarez government aud the United States, which will cover all disputed points. The best understanding prevails between the two governments. Senor Mata is perfectly satisfied that the President is determined to extend every aid in his

power to the liberal government of Mexico. The President has rccoguized Fianz August llersch as Consul at Boston, and Friederich Wilhelm Keutgen as Consul at New York, both for the free city of Bremen. There is but little if any doubt, from ciieutnstances which have recently transpired, that n convention or treaty between the United States and Mexico will soou be concluded, aud received here from Minister McLane early in September, in which event Senor Lerdo will return to New York, with a view to conclude the pecuniary arrangements already initiated by him, instead ol first lay iug his plans before the Juarez government, as ho originally intended. This treaty will probably be confined mainly to the Uuited States transit over Mexican territory, with certain commercial privileges or exemption from customs duties iu that connection, together with provision for adequate rneaus of protection. It is confidently asserted that the compensation for these advantages can easily be rendered mutually satisfactory. Other treaties will be proposed at one time, and iu these arrangements there is no reason to doubt provision will be made for the satisfaction of the Amei icau claims against Mexico. Distinguished friends of the Juarez government, including a number of Mexicans now here, regard the latest Mexican news as additionally encouraging to the cause of the constitutionalists, and speak of the excommunication of that party by the Archbishop of Mexico as a harmless proceeding.

The city article of the London Times says, in regard to the stipulations of the treaty alleged to have been arranged between Minister McLane aud Juarez, at Vera Cruz, that Mexico, will, from the moment the treaty is ratified, virtually pass under American sway, says the result will be advantageous to Mexico and the world, but the extent to which private rights will be respected or jeopardised is au anxious question. The American government is urged at every step to protect the iuterest of foreigu bondholders.

From the Barbados þÿ West Indian.'' RESULTS OF EMANCIPATION. Although few persons in this country, who have paid the smallest attention to the subject, believe that emancipation has not been perfectly successful, it is well, from time to time, to furnish them with additional evidence to strengthen their convictions. We have been permitted to publish the following extracts from a letter addressed to the late Mr. Joseph Sturge, from Barbados, under date of the 5th May last,

the writer of which is a man of mark in the island, occupying a high position, and to whose testimony implicit credence may be given : þÿ þÿ There can be no question þÿ there is none amongst any class of persons hero as to the þÿ beneficial results of emancipation in this island in every point of view. All classes participate, less or more, in its benefits, aud none more than the planters themselves. The people are generally well behaved, industrious, anxious to improve their condition by every means iu their power, aud never unwilling to work as long as they can hold up, whenever a fair inducement is offered to them. For a kind, considerate employer they are ever ready to do all their could be reasonably expected of men in that circumstances; for one that is barely just to them, that pays them regularly aud ungrudgingly for their labour, and is not on the alert to take advantage of them at every turn, they never object to work for fair wages ; aod even those of an opposite character fiud little difficulty, under ordinary circumstances, to get their lands cultivated and the work of their estates done. This being the character of the emancipated slaves as a body in this island þÿ a character which no one at all acquainted with them will refuse to accord them þÿ is it reasonable to suppose that the people of the very same race in the other colonies are naturally and essentially different in their character? that, with fair inducements to labour, they are idle? that,

with kind, considerate treatment, they are refractory, abusing the indulgence which they cannot appreciate ? that they care not to better their condition, neglect the opportunities that offer to that end, and utterly indifferent as to the future, and limit their exertions to the mere gratification of the present ? How can we the concile this picture with that presented by restate of things here in Barbados ? The difficulty is surely not overcome by saying, as the write! s opposed to us do, that Barbados is au exception to the other colouies This is not to account for the supposed vasi difference in the character of the same race of people iu those other colonies and Barbados, but to evade the question at the outset. There is, iu fact, no truth iu the character given to the labourers in the other colonies as regards their alleged idleness and unwillingness to work, their want of thrift, their indifference to future comfort iu an improved condition, and their care for only present gratification. They simply prefer giving their exertions in that direction which appears most profitable to them, aud, generally speaking, will only work for hiie in the plantations when they cant do better-, in other words, they look to their own interests in the matter rather than to the interests of the planters ; and this is, 1 apprehend, a very common trait of human nature everywhere. The planter wauts labour to for cul- it: tivate bis fields, aud otters a certain sum the negro has labour to dispose of, and can turn

it to beitor account iu tome other direction ; he therefore refuses the offer of the planter, and forthwith he is slandered as an idler, a vagabond, a most pestilent fellow, whom it were purely mawkish sentimentality to keep any terms with. Tax him, of course, in liis food, his clothing, his implements of labour, the lumber he builds or repairs his hut with, the medicines he administers to his wife and children in siiktiess þÿ in a word, tax him, right aud left, to supply the poor planter with the labour which he tefuscs to render. þÿ Did it never occur to you as somewhat strange, that, with the alleged great scarcity ol labour in the colonies, clamouring for immigration, wages continue all but stationary at what must be admitted to be very low rates ? In accordance with an admitted law, everything else rises with a short supply, but wages þÿol labour remain the same. The planter, in fact, has quite made up his mind to give only a certain rate of wages, what hr. thinks sufficient for the negro, who has þÿ few þÿwants, and ho measures the supply of labour by the readiness with which he can obtain it at this fixed rate. With quite as much justness might one of your manufacturers declare that no operatives in his line of business were to be had iu Birmingham, because, fixing a lower price for their labour than the state of the labour market justified, they could not be got to work with him for that.

( From the London Times, August 16 J If Sismondi could continue his great work to the present day, or if Machiavelli weie alive to write the history of Florence from the death of Lorenzo to the year 1860, the events that are now passing would furnish materials for a story altogether different from anything they had previously discussed. Instead of leading us along the little interesting track of internal wars, or testing our patience by involving us in the labyrinth of obscure domestic iutrigues, they would have to show us the unwonted spectacle of Princes appealing to the people, and the people gravely determining by an orderly vote by whom they would be governed. Italy ha'- got thus far. Once in ten years the destinies of the country seem to vibrate between absolute submission to the power of some great Sovereign and the exercise of voting by universal suffrage. It is hard to say which is the more pitiable condition. The chronic wearing disease of tyranny is perhaps more enduring, and the sharp imflammatory action of anarchy is quicker in its operation and more sudden in its passage ; but, in reality, both are diseases leading to the same end ; both tend eventually to the dissolution of the body politic. The moderate party in Italy know very well what universal suffrage in the choice of a Government means. It certain y means that they shall have no part in the decision. Tuscany has with wise promptitude taken her measures a before she has been brought under the pressure of any foreign force, and she has taken care that

her vote shall not be the vote of the ignorant and superstitious peasantry, recording the commands of their scarcely less ignorant but much less superstitious priests, but shall bo an emanation of the will of the active, intelligent, and thiukiug members of the community. In some States of Am'erica we believe a sort of compromise is made between democratic institutions and the peculiar institution of Slavery. The black man is not entirely ignored as a man ; he has his vote, or his portion of a vote, but the master exercises it for him. So it would now be in Italy if the country were polled from end to end, and every peasant and every mendicant had a vote, and if the priests were put in action and sustained by garrisons judiciously distributed. All this is now reduced to a system ; the machinery thoroughly is well understood, and, with the proper arrangements duly prepared, universal suffrage will turn you out a Government of any particular pattern as readily as a Manchester loom will produce the design to which it was set. This would not be so perhaps in England, for here the landowners and the manufacturers would fight it out with workmen on one sido and peasants on the other ; but in Ireland, or Spain, or Italy, or in the rural districts of Franco þÿ in every Catholic country where there is an ignorant peasantry to work withal þÿ there is no difficulty in working a mock popular election. This consideration detracts considerably from the confidence with which we note the answer of the French Emperor to

the deputations that are now thronging about him, and beseeching him not to force back upon them their old tyrants. The Elect of France naturally replies, that it is not for him, the jliosen of the French people, to force upon any people a Sovereign contrary to their will. The Emperor can easily afford to assure the suppliants from Tuscany that nothing shall be douo to prevent the full and absolute operation of the will of the people. The question remains, þÿ A people thus buffeted by adverse influences, who is to elect ? With absolute universal suffrage Napoleon III. could force any Prince he might chooso to name upon any Italian State just as easily as a conjuror could force a card upon a wondering clown in a provincial assembly-room. All that is required would bo to make his previous arrangement with the priests, and perhaps to have troops enough at hand to prevent any noisy demonstrations from the indignant minority. There arc always fools enough in Italy ready to afford excuse for an interference þÿ in the interests of þÿorder. What has just happened at Parma is quite enough. We recommend tho Tuscans not to rejoice and to be confident until they receive the Imperial ratification of all that has yet been done. We should bo glad to see the election of the reasonable and authoritative Convention, which oomprebends the name of every man of wealth and genius in Tuscany, confirmed by that sanction which can alone in the present crisis give it real power. It would be consolatory to know that there is

tured. They have not only to choose their Prince, but they have to determine, without tire i day must come ? possibility of any formal legal determination, the constitution of that assembly by which that Prince shall be chosen. Moreover, they are j working under the mioroscope of hostile criti- ! cism. would have meditated on the lesson which met him upon the threshold of his power. He had beheld the risks that beset the intemperate exercise of absolute power ; we expected him, therefore, to be liberal and concilatory. COMMUNICATION. j To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis ! Sir, In the dull, I might almost say, lethargic state, in which our community is at present plunged, there seems to be a good opportunity for directing our minds a little to our public affairs, and to discuss them in the only manner in which discussions on public affairs can lead to results, namely through the press. It has often appeared to me, that our citizens have either undervalued the benefits of having a press, or have been too timid in using it. True, the censorship is yet in full force here, although abolished in the mother country, and although the law abolishing it there was by Government laid before the Colonial Council here and recommended for their acceptance, which was unanimously given ; yet the Danish Government refused their assent to the law being passed here, and so the censorship, (his Popish institution of the dark ages, yet exists here. So much for the glory of the Colonial Council. But the censorship, like all other despotic inventions, can in an enlightened country never be wielded with its original rigour, for it is moderated by the spirit of the age, which influences the power that wields it. Thus will it be found, that the censorship will prove no impediment to a discussion on all and any of our public affairs, if the discussion be carried on without odious personalities. But, at the same time, I think, that the first step to be taken in our legislation, should be for the total liberatiou of tbe press. As since my return to the Island, I have had

plenty of lei.-ure time to meditato on matters and things generally, and to make comparisons with what I have seen and learned during my stay in America, I have thought it might be of some interest, and may be utility, if I commenced a series of articles in this paper on our

local matters, which hardly no oue has studied more than I, and to þÿw hich I can bring a long experience from the different stations and occupations I have held. I consider the present time as very propitious for this undertaking, the Colonial Council being soon about to assemble, and matters of grave importance coming also shortly before the Burgher Council. It may be objected, and with great appearance of reason, that the near meeting of tho Colonial Council and the bi-monthly discussions of the Burgher Council, would deprivo my labor of its object, or, will at least, render it useless,. Far from it The Colonial Council I thought almost dead, and the present attempt at resuscitating it, will doubtless prove abortive. I shall in a subsequent article show how the so-called Colonial Law was conceived and brought forth in so faulty a manner, that it began to decay as soon as born ; and it possessed so little innate vitality', that before the expiration of 10 years it will be numbered among tho things that wore. Therefore, to suggest an institution to replace the Colonial Council will be one of the first and most important of the subjects I propose to discuss. And, as to the Burgher Council, þÿ I would just now say no more of this respectable body, than that they hold the keys of a well-filled money chest, how to apply the money to a good purpose. be with that Council and its members. My lucubrations will not disturb them in tbeir labour of good, but these their labors will surely not render a public discus-

sion less available. Tho matters which I intend principally to discuss will embrace the legislation, administration, taxation in all its guises, the administration of law, the police, and the system or systems in use here for working the Estates; besides, all such other local matters, as may from time to time present themselves to the public attention, or be suggested to me. I shall lie thankful for any such suggestions from anybody, aud I shall be equally thankful for being corrected where I may fall in error. As I write from inclination only, theie will not be any regular publication of my ideas, but, the printer permitting, I will write, whenever my time allows it and my mind is given to it, my ideas on Matters and Things generally. HEILBUT11. St. Croix, Sept 1859.

From Chambers's Journal. SCIENCE AND ARTS. Among the freshest and most interesting of scientific topics, are certain facts concerning which our geologists are in a sta , ot surprise and excitement; so much so, that an extraordinary meeting of the Geological Society was head to discuss the matter. One is the discovery of flint implements þÿ knives and axe-lteaus þÿ near Amiens, at the bottom of a stratum of gravel, and from nineteen to twenty-five leet below the surface. The things have been actually louud in situ þÿ some by English gt ologisls þÿ where there is no appearance of the gravel ever having been previously disturbed ; and what is more remarkable, in a spot which forms the top of a hill The implements are in great numbers ; and tho conclusion is, that they testify to the existence of man on the earth, at a period anterior to that commonly supposed, thus confirming similar conclusions diawu Imm the discoveries made in the Brixham cave, and elsewhere. The other fact is one which we have heretofore incidentally mentioned: the exploration of a cave, Grotta di Maceagnone, near Palermo, by Dr. Falconer, where bones of extinct species of animals were found in astonishing quantities, along with fragments ol charcoal, aud knives of flint and agate in great number imbedded in the breccia The importance of this discovery may be judged of from the tact that hippopotami appear to have swarmed on the

spot. Of the bone known to anatomists as the astragalus, Dr Falconer picked up nearly a hundred examples within the space of a few teet ; and this bone is so easy of identification, as to leave no room for doubt. The existence of tho bonus has long been known to the natives, who have at times taken from the ancient 6tore to burn into ivory-black; but this is the first scientific investigation that has been made of the interesting deposit. Submarine telegraph is making good progress: another cablo is to be laid from the coast of Norfolk to Touuing, in Denmark þÿ three hundred aud eighty-eight miles. The benefit of the Red Sea telegraph has been already felt in the earlier arrival of the Indian advices by nearly a week. There would have been direct communication ere this from Aden to London thiough Constantinople, had not a temporary failure occurred in the attempt to lay a Hue from Al xaudria to Camlia. It is probable that by to,- time these lines appear in print, the failure will have been rectified, aud it will bo scarce a figure of speech to say that the West shakes hands with tho East. A line is to be laid from Sicily to Malta ; aud it appears that another trial is to be made to span the great ocean, by a new Atlantic telegraph company with a guarantee from government. Guicled by experience, they intend to use the lightest and at the same time strongest form of cable ; and if the Gieat Eastern should become available before the autumnal-equinox sets in, a new trial may be

made with reasonable chance of success. Meantime, certain experimentalists are busy with what they call the Globe telegraph ; that is, they seud the signal through the earth, and only use uu insulated wire for the return current. The signal current is generated by plates of iron, platinum, and zinc, buried in the ground, and is sufficiently powerful to produce a deflection of the needles, irrespective, as tho experimenters say, of distance. Certain physiologists at Paris have been tryiug experiments with a view to prove that, by the administration of drugs to a mother to þÿuft ect her milk, a weakly child may bo restored to health. The experiments have been tried on cows, aud by long-eoutinued doses, an effect has been produced, which hitherto has been thought beyoud the reach ofmedicino. þÿ Certain chemists are still at work on experiments for the discovery ot a compound that shall resemble the paucreatio secretion. This secretion, as physiologists know, is highly important in the process of digestion or assimilation of food, and if sotuo medicament could be found similar in quality, there would be at once an end to that distressing malady, indigestion. These investigations gre characteristic of tho progress of scientific medicine, and we heartily wish them success. It succes-ful, we may liopo that fraudulent imitators will leave them alono, for only by absolute purity of the preparation will cures be possible. þÿ Dr. Edward Smith has read papers before the Medical and Cbirurgical Society,

shewing that the human body is subject to cyclical changes which are not sufficiently taken into account by medical practitioners and hospital attendants who commonly pursue an unvarying mode of treat m nt. As regards the respiratory pheuotuetia, he shews that they are not so energetic iu summer as in winter ; and that those and other changes have more to do with the progress of disease than the meteorological influences which are not unfrcqucntly said to he implicated. Professor Dove, of Berlin, has published a short paper on the use of the stereoscope iu the detection of forgeries, whether commercial or literary. By placing the suspected document, aud comparing it with a known original under the stereoscope, tho difference is manifest at once, for the slightest variation of space between words or lines, the slightest difference of position in au engraving, are immediately detected. The method is applicable to drawings and engravings, to printed books and bank-notes ; and honest men will rejoice in a discovery which increases the difficulty of falsification. þÿWheatstono smirror-stereoscope is tho one that should be used ; aud those who try the experiment will be surprised to see how some of the lines seem to start forward, and others to recode, according as they disagree in position.

$L CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 20tii SEPTEMBER, 1859. þÿ þÿ Arrival of the Packet. Tiie Royal Mail Steamer Parana arrived at St. Thomas on Saturday last with London dates to the 2nd inst., which are, however, barren of political news. The hopes entertained in France that the Conference of Zurich would have been brought u> a successful termination by the end of the last month, are far from being realised. The chances of arranging are stated to bo so slight as to render a dissolution of the Conference very probable. A Congress of war seems to some the only alternative; but to this Austria is op- posed. " The Duchies", says the Times, " are a great difficulty, aud there appears no possibility of a settlement. The Emperors are agreed as to the propriety, or rather necessity, of restoring the two Dukes, but diverge on the means of setting about it. Austria employ would not, perhaps, object to force. France will only ' moral suasion,' which does not appear to have made much progress; while Piedmont is still ready, we are told, to accept the annexation spontaneously offered. Now, the case is this If Piedmont annex, will Austria recommence the war ; and if Austria recommences the war, will France once more fly to the relief of an old ally ? These are questions to be asked. In official quarters, I may add, a better colouring is tried to be given to things. One there learns that matters are going on ' as well as can be expected ;' but that if important points are not settled at Zurich, important points were not meant to be set-

tled there, but rather before a Congress. In the mean time Prince Napoleon is reported to be more than discontented with the turn matters have taken ; he proposes to leave Paris for some remote part of France,
to lay aside even his armorial bearings, to quit the busy scenes of politics and pleasure, and lead tho life of a hermit. Such, at all events, are the on dits of the Palais Royal.

We are able from an official source to publish a series of drafts of Ordinances which it is the intention of Government to lay before tb 3 Colonial Council in its session this year, together with the motives on which they are based. Among those drafts of Ordinances, are, we understand, the following: 1, Draft of the Budget for the Danish Westindia Possessions for the financial period from the 1st of April 1860 to the 31st of March 1861 ; 2, Draft of a Law relating to trade and navigation in St. Thomas (this draft of a Law is the same as vyas laid before the Colonial Council in its session in 185 1, with several additionsand changes, and among these a clause enacting the reduction of the duties on Colonial produce). 3, Draft of an Ordinance modifying the Postal Ordinance of 10th July 1855; 4, Draft of an Ordinance modifying and adding certain clauses to the Ordinance of 6th Sept. 1853 for the regulation of the Country Schools in the Danish Westindia Possessions ; 5, Draft of an Ordinance prohibiting vessels running into other landing places in the Danish Westindia Possessions, than the authorized harbours. 6, Draft of an Ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Islands the haw of 29th Decbr, 1857, concerning the majority at law of females ; 7, Drafi of an Ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Islands the Law of 29th Decbr. 1857, modifying the Ordinance of 21 et May 1845, concerning the right of inheritance ; 8, Draft of an Ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Possessions the Law of the 29th Decbr.

1857 enacting that funds belonging to minors, and not exceeding 100 Rd. are in future not to be given in trust to the Upperguardians etc. ; 9, Draft of an Ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Possessions the Law of 29th December 1857 by which J 3 of the Ordinance of 30th April 1824, concerning the duties of clergymen with regard to marriages has been changed; 10, Draft of an Ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Possessions the Law of 30th Novbr. 1857 exacting that baptism slial I no longer be a condition for the right of inheritance ; 11, Draft of an Ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Possessions the Law of 30th Novbr. 1857 concerning summons to creditors in dealings (Proclaniata) ; 12, Draft of an Ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Possessions the Law of 21st January 1857 concerning the punishment for illtrcatment of animals; 13, Draft of an Ordinance mollifying tiie Royal Rescript of 9th December 1825 3, concerning tiie aimullation in Court of bonds that have been lost.

Until within ten years ago, the kingdom of Denmark presented in theory the most absolute- þÿ ly ruled country in the world. The in lex þÿregia of November 14, 1665, established, place of the ancient liberties voluntarily surrendered by the nation with the view of obtaining a better constitution to bo framed by the kiug, a Government so thoroughly absolute, as to exceed even oriental despotisms in its principle ; for, while in these latter, the sovereign enjoyed a full and uncontrolled power to rule according to any principle or no principle at all, the to Danish and was bound by the lex regia rule sovereign govern in the most absolute and uncontrolled manner possible ; so that, while the form of government iu eastern monarchies depended merely on the will of the ruler, and could by him, or sometimes by his subjects, be altered for the better, þÿ it was in Denmark founded on a solemn law, which called itself unalterable, and which declared it high treason, punishable with death, infamy and confiscation of property, even to speak of any alteration in this form of Government. However, while such was the legal state of things, or the principle of Government in theory, it was much different in its practical application. For, flic Danes, enjoying from the earliest ages an almost unbounded freedom, could ill bear a despotic rule ; and so well was this feeling known The election will he closed at 3 þÿo clock and respected by tlio Government, that the lex regia, although enacted in the year 1665, was
not published until the year 1709, for fear of rousing the people. It must also be acknow-

ledgcd, that, although uncontrolled in their unlimited absolute sovereignty, the Danish kings exercised on the whole a mild and moderate sway. This state of things subsisted until, after the French revolution of 1830, it was found to be no longer tenable. The king, Frederik VI, then instituted the Provincial Diets, which first assembled in 1834 These assemblies had only a consultative voice, given within closed doors, and they were meant to have no political power whatever. But it was soon found, that the ancient spirit of freedom was not dead among the Danes'; for no sooner had the Provincial Diets raised their voice, than this spirit awoke from one end in Denmark to the other; and thus it became possible, that in the short space of 14 years from the first assembling of these Diets, by their activity and firmness, aided by the enlightened moral force of a whole nation panting for its liberties, the absolutist principle of Government in Denmark was subverted without resistance and without disturbauce, and the Danish people and their noble King agreed to a most liberal constitution Meanwhile, the Danish Colonies, unaffected by the changes at home, contiuued under the absolute rule of the king and the yet more absolute rule of his governors. This was possible as long as the Provincial Diets bad only consultative votes, the form of Government remaining absolute in principle. But, as soon as this form was succeeded by a constitutional regime, then the Colonies could no longer continuo to be

governed in an absolute and irresponsible manner, the minister having charge of the colonial affairs being a constitutional and responsible minister, he could not, of course, at the same time be absolute and irresponsible for one branch of his functions, as little as the king, after having adopted the constitutional regime, could retain an absolute rule for any single part of his kingdom. For that His Majesty is even now the absolute ruler in his duchies of Holstein and Lauenborg, cannot be argued against this truth, these duchies neither belonging to Denmark, nor being under the Danish Government, whereas these colonies belong exclusively to the Kingdom of Denmark properly so called, and are ruled by the Government of the Kingdom. There is another fact that might be adduced to prove the feasibility of constitutional States possessing colonies which are excluded from participation in the constitutional rule of the mother-country, and arc governed in the most absolute, arbitrary and irresponsible manner, viz: the Spanish colonies. But this fact cannot bo adduced as argument in our case, thoir circumstances being in every respect different from ours, the constitution of Spain beiug a sham, and the Spanish colonies, which every Spaniard considers as milch cows only, being governed on that principle. The Danish Government, being then really constitutional, they saw the necessity of extending that system to the colonies. (To be continued.)
