might be, that relief received by a young person in his 16th þÿ and 17th year, for instance by his being laid in a Hospital at the public cost on account of the fracturing of a limb, could, on account of his having previously supported himself from his 15ih year, become an obstacle to his marriage in his 20th year, allhough this would Dot be the case according to the law existing in the mother-country. It has theiefore been a matter of consideration whether, in extending þÿ words : during the last 5 þÿyears , the words, the law to these islands, after the þÿ but after his having filled his 18th þÿyear ought not to be added, by doing which a perfect uuity between the effects ol the law, as in the mother-country, and in these islands, would be gained, and likewise a fixed age, which would lessen those difficulties which clergymen will have in procuring such authentic elucidations on the question whether the person has received pauper-relief as they, in accordance with the Ordinance of 30tli April 1824, 4 must procure. Weightier reasons have however been found against inserting t lie above addition in extending the law to tlio Dani.-h Weslindia Possessions, as, considering local circumstances, the age of 15 would be a more proper age at which the right of receiving relief as a child should terminate, than the age of 18, which would furthermore be in analogy with the provisional ordinance of 26th Jauuary 1849 l for St. Croix, þÿ and that at the same time it must be admitted that the present Ordinance treating

,especially on the influence of having received pauper-relief as a hindrance to marriage, ought to be in unison with the general rules existing here with regard to pauper-relief, in the same manner, as the hitherto existing enactments iu the Ordinance of 30th April 1824 3, No. 10) and not introduce an especial deviation from these.

From the Barbados Westindian. We trust, in the interests of humanity, that tins condition of the Chinese Immigrants in Cuba, as described by Mr Foderingham, iu his Letter published in the lafct West Indian, will awaken the sympathy of the British Public, and open their eyes to the real nature ot the trade till recently, þÿ perhaps still carried on in British first-class Steam and Clipper Ships. The Chinese, Mr. Foderingham says, are, on their ar- rival at II vanu, sold at 300 dollars per head to . the Planters, and sent away into the oonntry to work on the Sugai Estates, and to be treated in every respeot like tbe African Slaves, to be watched, lodged, f. d, chained, flogged, imprisoned, and worked to death þÿ without cessation day and night, Sundays and all, to the extent of humau euduiauce. The Chinese are treated like the Africans ; and there seems to be no difference between the treatment of the slaves and that of the cattle on the estates, which are in the nose, and a pointed goad kept for purposes of draught, with to an iron them prick ring on. The Chinese and Africans are treated exactly the same as the brute beasts Christians. by men who profess themselves in Cuba, One of these monster Sugar Manufactories, clearing its two or three hundred thousand dollars yearly, must be a perfect hell upon earth. One thousand human beings are made to toil, suffer every kind of anguish, and perish gradually from overwork, like brute beasts, to produce this golden harvest for one man, or for a few who form themselves into a company

to raise the capital necessary to carry on the bu-imss. Here we see, in all its nakedness, the cruelty of Avarice. Labor is the lot of all ; wealth is honorable; but every humane mind must recoil Iroin wealth acquired by such means. These miserable Chinese are decoyed from their own country, and brought across the ocean, under false promises and expectations. We have Seen them here in Barbados, on board Briti-b Ships, on their way to tbe Havana, crowding the decks and rigging, and appearing cheeriul and happy, as described by Mr. Foderingliam, unconscious ot the wretched fate that awaited them Cannot something be done for these wretched people to mitigate their sufferings, if not to procure justice tor them, and to rescue them from slavery ? In former times the Slave Code of the Spaniards was distinguished from those of other nations, by its greater respect for tbe laws of humanity. Tbe slaves were recognised and treated as fellowmen, if not I'eliow-christians ; but now they are put upon the same footing with the beasts of burthen, and worked systematically to get the greatest amount ol labor out of them in the shortest time The system is truly diabolical ; how it ran be suffered to exist iu a civilized and pi olessedly Christian couutiy, passes our understanding. The Chinese are first decoyed, then cheated, enslaved, oppressed, aud diiven to commit suicide, þÿ the most common form being by hanging themselves, for which we are gravely informed greater facilities exist than for other

modes of getting rid of their miserable lives They are not permitted the use of women ; they are severely punished for smoking ; aud every precaution is takeu to preveut them committing suicide Work, work, work, like the horses, the mules, and the cattle, kept on the Estates. The Chinese and the Hindoo Coolies are brought too to work on the Sugar Estates ill the British Colonics ; they are carried in great numbers to the Mauritius, and already form a distinct portion of the population iu Guiana, Trinidad, Jamaica, and some other of these Islands Are they treated in the same way as Mr. Immigrants Foderingham d.-seribes the treatment of the into Cuba ? The condition of tbo Immigiants in the British Colonies contrasts siruiigly with what it is in tbe Island of Cuba. The precautions taken by the British Government agaiust their ill-treatment, are wanting there. The Governors of the Colonies are their protectors; besides whom, there is an Inspector of Immigrants, aud Magistrates specially appointed to hear their complaiuts, aud to see the contracts into which they have entered, faithfully executed by their employers. An amended Immigration Act lias recently passed iu Grenada, þÿ to authorise the cancelling by the Governor of the indenture of aDy immigrant ill-used by his employer, or in case of breach of contract by either party. It repeals clause 36 of the. Immigration Aot, 1855 ; and it enables the Governor in Council, from time to time, to regulate the form of application for immigrants; the

lodging, medicine, medical aid, care, food and clothing to be provided, and the general treatment of the immigrants ; the periods within which their wages shall be paid; and to alter or vary the form of any contract, indenture, list, must. r roll, return, or specifications continued in the said Act, and to substitute þÿothers. Alter the termination of the period of service they are permitted to enter into a new contract, or if they please, to return to their native coun try with their savings, þÿ often amounting to several hundred dollars, back passage being a provided for them by the Colony. How different this to the treatment they experience in Cuba, where they are made to work like slaves, and if by chance they pass through the dreadful ordeal, the greatest jealousy is entertained of their remaining in the country, and it is seriously proposed, according to Mr. Foderingham, to compel them either to leave it, or to enter into a new contract. We hope that the statement of such an unexceptionable witness, and on the respeotable authority of Mr. Foderingham, will bring this subject to the notice of the British public and the Anti-Slavery and other Philanthropic Societies in England, through whose interference something may be done to check, or to lessen the shamef ul state of thing alluded to.

debted to it lor having maintained vigorously, in all its purity, the honour of the Austrian flag It is not less perfectly established that our enemies, in spite of the present efforts, in spite of the superior forcos which they had for a long period been preparing for the conflict, have been able even by making the greatest sacrifices, to obtain only advantages, not a decisive victory ; while the Austrian army, still animated by the same ardour, and full of the same courage, maintained a position, the possession of which left perhaps a possibility of recovering from the enemy all the advantages that he had gained But for this purpose it would have been necessary to make new sacrifices, which certainly would not have been less bloody than those which have been made already, and which have deeply afflicted my heart. ol Lombardy.
